concepts.in_practice: A platform team usually starts by picking one real model and building a thin end-to-end path for it: a pipeline definition in an orchestrator, a tracked training run, a registered model, an automated evaluation gate and a deployment with basic monitoring. They then turn that path into templates other teams can copy. Reviews focus on the seams: is the data validated before training, is the model compared against the production baseline, can any deployed model be traced to its data and commit, and what triggers retraining. Maturity is raised stage by stage where the pain is highest, not everywhere at once.

sources.title: MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning
Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems

body.body: A production ML system moves through data extraction, data validation, data preparation, model training, model evaluation, model validation, serving and monitoring. Each stage produces an artifact the next one consumes: a dataset snapshot, a feature set, a trained model file, an evaluation report, a deployed endpoint. The platform view is to treat every stage as a pipeline step with declared inputs and outputs, so it can be rerun, cached and audited. Monitoring closes the loop, because signals from production such as data drift or falling accuracy are what trigger a new run.
body.heading: Stages and artifacts

body.body: Three things change together in ML: code, data and model. A release can break with no code change at all, because the input distribution moved. Testing therefore covers data schemas and value ranges, model quality against a baseline, and the serving infrastructure itself. Deployment is often a multi-step pipeline that deploys another service, the prediction service, instead of a single binary. Teams also include researchers who are not primarily software engineers, so the platform has to make the correct path the easy one.
body.heading: Why it differs from ordinary software

subtopics.title: The lifecycle stages and what flows between them

body.body: A widely used model describes three levels. At level 0 everything is manual: notebooks, a hand-trained model passed to engineers, infrequent releases and no monitoring. At level 1 the training pipeline itself is automated and deployed, which enables continuous training: the pipeline reruns on a schedule, on new data, or on a drift trigger, with automated data and model validation. At level 2 the pipeline code has its own CI/CD system, so new pipeline components are built, tested and rolled out automatically. Level 1 adds a feature store, a metadata store and pipeline triggers as supporting components.
body.heading: Level 0 to level 2

body.body: The levels are useful for deciding what to build next, not as a score. A team with a handful of models that rarely change may be well served at level 0 with good versioning. The move to level 1 pays off when retraining is frequent or the data shifts quickly. Level 2 matters when many people change pipelines and experiments need to reach production fast. A sound first step in most organisations is one end-to-end pipeline that is simple but fully automated, then improving each stage.
body.heading: Using the model as a roadmap

subtopics.title: Maturity levels: manual, pipeline automation, CI/CD automation

body.body: Continuous integration in ML tests and validates data, data schemas and models in addition to code. Continuous delivery ships a training pipeline, which in turn ships a prediction service, so there are two delivery targets. Continuous training is the ML-specific addition: the system retrains and redeploys models automatically. Typical triggers are a schedule, the arrival of new data, a drop in model performance, or a significant change in data distributions. Each automated run needs gates: data validation decides whether to train at all, and model validation decides whether the new model may replace the current one.
body.heading: What each term means for ML

subtopics.title: CI, CD and continuous training

body.body: The classic paper on this topic argues that ML systems carry all the maintenance problems of ordinary code plus ML-specific ones. Entanglement means changing one input feature changes the behavior of everything else. Unstable or underused data dependencies are harder to detect than code dependencies. Feedback loops arise when a model influences its own future training data. Glue code and pipeline jungles grow around general-purpose packages, and configuration becomes a large, untested surface. The model code itself is a small box in the middle of serving infrastructure, data collection, feature extraction, monitoring and resource management.
body.heading: Sources of debt

body.body: Platform work is largely debt prevention. Shared pipeline components replace glue code. Schema checks and data validation catch dependency changes at the boundary. Versioned, reviewed configuration replaces ad hoc flags. Monitoring of prediction distributions and input features detects silent failures. Practical guidance from large ML teams adds: launch with a simple model and solid infrastructure first, test the infrastructure independently from the model, and watch for training-serving skew by logging features at serving time and reusing them for training.
body.heading: What a platform does about it

subtopics.title: Hidden technical debt in ML systems

body.body: A model is reproducible when the code version, the data version, the configuration and the environment that produced it can all be recovered. Code goes in Git. Data is versioned by immutable snapshots or by a data versioning tool that stores pointers alongside the code. Models are stored in a registry with lineage back to the run that produced them. Environments are pinned through locked dependencies and container image digests. An ML metadata store records each pipeline run: parameters, input artifacts, output artifacts and metrics, which makes it possible to compare runs, debug regressions and roll back.
body.heading: The three axes

subtopics.title: Reproducibility: versioning code, data and models

concepts.summary: MLOps applies DevOps discipline to systems whose behavior depends on data and trained artifacts as well as code. The lifecycle runs from data preparation through training, evaluation, release and monitoring, then loops back through retraining. The platform engineer's job is to make that loop automated, reproducible and observable, so that model code is only a small part of a well-run system.
concepts.title: MLOps and the ML lifecycle: from experiment to production system

concepts.in_practice: Teams standardise on a project template: a src layout, a pyproject.toml with pinned tool settings, a lock file, a test folder and a container build that installs from the lock. Shared platform code lives in a small number of internal packages published to a private index by CI on tagged commits. Data scientists create environments with one command, and CI rebuilds the environment from scratch on every change so that drift between laptops and the cluster shows up as a failed build instead of a failed training run.

body.body: A virtual environment is a self-contained directory tree holding a particular Python version plus its own set of installed packages. It is created with the standard venv module, for example by running python -m venv .venv, and activated by a script that puts its bin directory first on the shell path. Packages installed with pip then go into that environment only. This solves the conflict where one application needs version 1 of a library and another needs version 2. The environment directory is disposable and should be excluded from version control; the list of requirements is what gets committed.
body.heading: How a virtual environment works

body.body: ML stacks have heavy native dependencies: numerical libraries, GPU runtimes and compiled extensions that are tied to specific driver and Python versions. Two projects on the same machine frequently cannot share one interpreter. In production the container image is the real isolation boundary, yet a virtual environment inside the image is still common because it keeps application packages apart from system Python. The platform rule is one environment per project, created from a declared file, never built up by hand.
body.heading: Why it matters more in ML

subtopics.title: Virtual environments and isolation

body.body: There are two lists to keep. The declared list states what the project needs directly, with version ranges. The resolved list, or lock file, records the exact version of every direct and transitive package that was actually installed. The simplest form is pip freeze writing a requirements.txt that pip install -r can replay. Dedicated tools produce lock files with hashes so that an install fails if a package was tampered with or changed. Training and serving should install from the same lock, since a different numerical library version between them is a real cause of training-serving skew.
body.heading: Declared versus resolved dependencies

subtopics.title: Dependency pinning and lock files

body.body: A distributable package has a pyproject.toml that names a build backend in its build-system table and holds metadata in the project table: name, version, required Python version, dependencies and entry points. A common layout puts importable code under a src directory, with tests beside it. Running the build frontend produces two artifacts: a source distribution and a wheel, which is a prebuilt archive pip can install without running build steps. Artifacts are uploaded to an index with an upload tool, and a test index exists for rehearsing a release before publishing for real.
body.heading: Project layout and build

body.body: Platform teams ship shared code as versioned packages instead of copying modules between repositories: a client for the feature store, pipeline step helpers, logging and tracing setup. These go to a private index, and consumers pin a version. Semantic versioning signals breaking changes, and console entry points in the project metadata turn the package into a command line tool that data scientists can run. Keeping the SDK thin, with few dependencies, avoids forcing version conflicts onto every training environment that installs it.
body.heading: Internal platform SDKs

subtopics.title: Packaging libraries with pyproject.toml

body.body: Platform Python code is tested in layers. Unit tests cover pure functions such as feature transforms and config parsing, using a test runner with fixtures and parametrised cases. Contract tests check that a pipeline step accepts and emits the expected schema. Integration tests run a miniature pipeline on a tiny dataset to prove the steps connect, which is cheap insurance against failures that would otherwise show up hours into a real run. CI runs these across the supported Python versions inside a fresh environment built from the lock file, so the test also verifies that the package installs cleanly.
body.heading: Test layers

subtopics.title: Testing platform and pipeline code

body.body: Type hints plus a static type checker catch a large class of errors before a job is ever scheduled, which matters when a failure costs GPU hours. A linter and formatter remove style debate and run as pre-commit hooks and in CI. Configuration, a known debt source in ML systems, is parsed into typed models at startup so a wrong learning rate type or a missing path fails fast with a clear message. Project templates bake all of this in, so every new repository starts with the same tool settings in its pyproject.toml.
body.heading: Static checks as a platform default

subtopics.title: Typing, linting and validated configuration

concepts.summary: Python is the common language of ML teams, so platform tooling, pipeline components and SDKs are mostly written in it. The platform concern is not syntax but engineering hygiene: isolated environments, reproducible dependencies, properly packaged libraries and tested code. Getting these right is what makes a training job behave the same on a laptop, in CI and on a cluster.
concepts.title: Python for platform engineering: packaging, environments and testing

concepts.in_practice: A platform team gives each ML team a namespace with quotas and offers two paved paths: a chart or template for an inference Deployment with correct probes and resource settings, and a job template for training with checkpoint paths, retry limits and GPU tolerations already filled in. Images are built in CI, pushed to a registry and referenced by digest. Researchers rarely write raw manifests; they submit through an SDK or orchestrator that generates Jobs, while the platform team watches pending pods, out-of-memory kills and image pull times as its core health signals.

body.body: A container image packages the application with its dependencies and runtime so it runs the same everywhere. ML images are unusually large because they carry numerical libraries, a deep learning framework and often GPU runtime libraries, so several gigabytes is normal. Layer ordering matters: put the base image and slow-changing dependencies first and the application code last, so rebuilds and node pulls reuse cached layers. Multi-stage builds keep compilers out of the final image. Model weights are usually kept out of the image and fetched from object storage at start, so that one image can serve many model versions.
body.heading: What makes ML images different

subtopics.title: Container images for ML code

body.body: A cluster has a control plane, with the API server, scheduler, controller managers and etcd, and worker nodes running the kubelet and a container runtime. Users declare objects and controllers reconcile actual state toward them. For ML the important extension is that this model is open: custom resources and operators add new object kinds such as a distributed training job or an inference service, and the same reconcile loop manages them. Kubernetes deliberately does not provide application-level services or dictate a CI system, which is the gap an ML platform fills.
body.heading: The parts that matter for ML

subtopics.title: Cluster model and desired state

body.body: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and performs rolling updates controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable. Model servers stress this mechanism because a pod may need minutes to pull a large image and load weights into memory. Readiness probes must only pass after the model is loaded, and a startup probe gives slow starts room without loosening liveness checks. Setting maxUnavailable to zero with a surge of one keeps capacity during rollout, at the price of needing a spare node, which is expensive when that node has a GPU. Rollback uses the revision history the Deployment keeps.
body.heading: Rollout behavior with slow-starting pods

subtopics.title: Deployments for model servers

body.body: A Job creates one or more pods and tracks them until a set number complete successfully. Key fields are completions and parallelism for fan-out work, backoffLimit for how many retries to allow, activeDeadlineSeconds to cap runtime, and ttlSecondsAfterFinished to clean up. Indexed completion mode gives each pod a stable index, useful for sharding a dataset across workers. A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule, a simple way to run periodic retraining or batch scoring. The pod restartPolicy must be Never or OnFailure, since a Job is not meant to run forever.
body.heading: Run-to-completion workloads

body.body: Nodes get drained, spot capacity gets reclaimed and pods get preempted, so a training job must tolerate restarts. The standard pattern is periodic checkpointing to object storage or a persistent volume and resuming from the latest checkpoint on start. Jobs should be idempotent, writing outputs to a path keyed by run id. A plain Job has no notion of several pods that must all start together, which is why distributed training uses operators and batch schedulers that add gang scheduling and queues on top of the Job primitive.
body.heading: Making training survive the cluster

subtopics.title: Jobs for training and batch inference

body.body: The scheduler places a pod on a node by its resource requests; limits cap what the container may use at runtime. Exceeding a memory limit gets the container killed, a frequent failure when a data loader or a model is larger than expected. Pods whose requests equal their limits get the Guaranteed quality of service class and are evicted last. GPUs appear as extended resources exposed by a device plugin, requested in the limits section as a whole number, and are not overcommitted by default. Node selectors, taints and tolerations keep ordinary pods off expensive GPU nodes.
body.heading: How scheduling decisions are made

subtopics.title: Resource requests, limits and GPUs

concepts.summary: Kubernetes is the default substrate for ML platforms because it schedules containers across a shared pool of machines and keeps declared state true. ML uses two workload shapes on it: long-running services for inference and run-to-completion jobs for training and batch work. This lesson covers the container and workload primitives that later lessons on GPUs, scheduling and serving build on.
concepts.title: Kubernetes for ML workloads: containers, deployments and jobs

concepts.in_practice: Teams define the whole foundation in infrastructure as code: VPC and subnets, the EKS cluster, add-on versions, node pools or autoscaler configuration, IAM roles and the service account mappings. A new ML team is onboarded by a module that creates a namespace, a service account, a scoped IAM role and a bucket prefix. Cluster upgrades are rehearsed in a non-production cluster first. The EKS best practices guide is used as the baseline for security, reliability, networking and scalability settings, and the ML Lens is applied when a new workload type goes to design review.

sources.title: Machine Learning Lens - AWS Well-Architected Framework

body.body: EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you across multiple availability zones and handles its scaling, patching and availability. The data plane is your choice: managed node groups of EC2 instances, self-managed nodes, Fargate for serverless pods, or modes in which AWS also automates node provisioning. Cluster capabilities come as add-ons such as the VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy and storage drivers, each with its own version to keep compatible. Upstream Kubernetes conformance means standard tooling and operators work unchanged. Version upgrades remain a team responsibility and need a rehearsed process, since Kubernetes versions leave standard support on a fixed schedule.
body.heading: What AWS manages and what the team manages

subtopics.title: EKS architecture and the responsibility split

body.body: IAM controls who is authenticated and what they are authorised to do. The pieces are principals (users, roles, federated identities), policies written as JSON documents that allow or deny actions on resources, and roles that are assumed to obtain temporary credentials. Roles with short-lived credentials are preferred over long-term access keys. Least privilege means granting only the actions and resources a task needs, for example read access to one bucket prefix for a training job.
body.heading: IAM building blocks

body.body: Pods should not inherit the broad role of the node they run on. Instead a Kubernetes service account is mapped to an IAM role, either through the cluster OIDC provider with a trust policy (IAM roles for service accounts) or through EKS Pod Identity associations. The AWS SDK inside the pod picks up temporary credentials automatically. On an ML platform this gives per-team and per-workload scoping: a training job can read its dataset and write its checkpoints, an inference service can only read model artifacts, and every access is attributable in audit logs.
body.heading: Giving a pod an AWS identity

subtopics.title: IAM and identity for pods

body.body: With the default VPC CNI each pod receives a real IP address from the VPC subnets, which makes pods directly routable but means large clusters consume addresses quickly. Subnet sizing therefore has to account for peak pod count, not node count, and options such as prefix delegation or secondary address ranges exist for when space runs short. Nodes normally sit in private subnets across several zones, with load balancers in front for ingress. VPC endpoints for object storage and the container registry keep heavy data and image traffic on the AWS network and avoid NAT gateway charges, which can be significant for dataset downloads.
body.heading: Pod networking and address planning

subtopics.title: VPC networking for EKS

body.body: ML clusters mix cheap general-purpose nodes for control and pipeline pods with accelerated instances for training and inference. Managed node groups give fixed pools per instance type backed by auto scaling groups. A node autoscaler such as Karpenter instead watches pending pods and launches instances that fit them directly, which suits bursty and heterogeneous GPU demand, and it can consolidate underused nodes. GPU nodes use accelerated machine images with drivers preinstalled and carry taints so only GPU workloads land there. Scaling GPU pools to zero when idle is one of the largest cost levers.
body.heading: Choosing how nodes appear

body.body: Spot capacity is far cheaper but can be reclaimed at short notice, so it fits checkpointed training and batch inference, not latency-critical serving. Capacity for specific GPU types is uneven across zones, and a job with a zonal persistent volume is pinned to that zone, which can leave it unschedulable. Common storage choices are object storage for datasets and model artifacts, block volumes for per-pod scratch, and shared file systems for datasets many pods read at once. Image pull time for large images is managed with registry caching and prewarmed nodes.
body.heading: Spot, zones and storage

subtopics.title: Compute and node strategy for ML

body.body: The Machine Learning Lens extends the AWS Well-Architected Framework to ML workloads. It walks through the ML lifecycle phases, from business goal identification and problem framing through data processing, model development, deployment and monitoring, and for each phase lists best practices under the framework pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability. It is cloud guidance, not a product, and is used as a checklist in design reviews. Typical findings concern missing lineage tracking, no rollback plan for a model, unscoped data access, and training resources that are not right-sized or not shut down.
body.heading: A review framework for ML workloads

subtopics.title: The Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens

concepts.summary: Amazon EKS is the managed Kubernetes service many ML platforms are built on: AWS runs the control plane and the team owns the workloads, the node strategy and the integrations. The foundations to get right are identity, networking, compute choice and storage, because ML workloads are heavy users of all four. The Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens gives a review framework for the resulting design.
concepts.title: AWS and EKS foundations for an ML platform

concepts.in_practice: A team keeps Spark transformations as plain functions from DataFrame to DataFrame in a Python package, tested locally in CI, and submits them through an orchestrator that passes the logical date. Each job reads date-partitioned Parquet or lakehouse tables, writes one output partition idempotently, and is followed by a data quality task. The platform group owns the base image, cluster or Kubernetes operator configuration, default tuning such as adaptive execution, and dashboards for job duration, shuffle size and cost per run. When a job slows down, the first step is the Spark UI: find the slowest stage, compare maximum and median task time, and check for skew, spill or a missing partition filter before adding hardware.

sources.title: Spark SQL, DataFrames and Datasets Guide

body.body: A Spark application has one driver and many executors. DataFrame transformations such as select, filter, join and groupBy are lazy: they only build a logical plan. An action such as write, count or collect makes the Catalyst optimizer rewrite that plan (predicate pushdown, column pruning, join reordering) and compile it to a physical plan. The plan is cut into stages at every shuffle boundary, and each stage runs one task per partition. Because DataFrames carry a schema, SQL and the DataFrame API go through the same optimizer and perform the same, which is why pipelines mix both freely.
body.heading: From DataFrame code to tasks

body.body: A partition is the slice of data one task processes in memory on one executor core. Too few partitions give huge tasks that spill to disk or fail with out-of-memory errors; too many give scheduling overhead and thousands of tiny output files. Input partitioning comes from the file layout, while post-shuffle partitioning is set by spark.sql.shuffle.partitions and, with adaptive query execution on, adjusted at runtime by coalescing small partitions. Reading the query plan with explain and the stage view in the Spark UI is the basic skill for reasoning about any slow job.
body.heading: Why partitions are the unit of everything

subtopics.title: Execution model: driver, executors, lazy plans

body.body: Most Spark cost is shuffle: moving rows across the network so that equal keys land in the same partition for a join or aggregation. A sort-merge join shuffles both sides; a broadcast hash join ships a small table to every executor and avoids the shuffle entirely, so keeping dimension tables under the broadcast threshold is a cheap win. Filtering and projecting before the join reduces shuffled bytes. Columnar formats such as Parquet let Spark skip columns and row groups at read time, so the cheapest optimization is often a better partition filter on the input.
body.heading: Where the time goes

body.body: Skew means a few keys hold most rows, for example a null user id or one very large customer. One task then runs for an hour while the other 199 finish in seconds, and it often dies on memory. Adaptive query execution can split skewed partitions in sort-merge joins automatically. When that is not enough, teams filter or separately handle the hot keys, salt the key with a random suffix on both sides, or pre-aggregate before joining. The symptom to look for in the Spark UI is a stage whose maximum task duration and shuffle read size are far above the median.
body.heading: Skew and how to handle it

subtopics.title: Shuffles, joins and data skew

body.body: PySpark is a Python API over the same engine: built-in functions in pyspark.sql.functions execute in the JVM and are optimized, while a plain Python UDF serializes every row to a Python worker and back and is opaque to the optimizer. The rule is built-in functions first, then pandas UDFs, which exchange Arrow batches and run vectorized code, and row-at-a-time UDFs last. The pandas API on Spark helps port pandas code, but the same shuffle and partition rules apply underneath.
body.heading: Staying in the JVM, and when you cannot

body.body: For high-volume unstructured data the usual pattern is to keep the heavy bytes in object storage and have Spark process a manifest table of paths plus metadata. Spark distributes the work with mapInPandas or a pandas UDF that opens each object, decodes it and emits embeddings, thumbnails or extracted attributes. Partition count is tuned by bytes per task instead of row count, because one row can be hundreds of megabytes. GPU inference inside such jobs needs executor resource requests and batch sizes sized to the device, and is often moved to a dedicated batch inference system.
body.heading: Images, video and point clouds

subtopics.title: PySpark for feature and unstructured data work

body.body: Structured Streaming treats a stream as a table that keeps growing and runs the same DataFrame query incrementally, by default in micro-batches. A source such as Kafka or a file directory supplies offsets, the engine processes new rows, and a sink receives the result in append, update or complete output mode. Progress and state are written to a checkpoint location; on restart the query resumes from the recorded offsets. With a replayable source and an idempotent or transactional sink this gives end-to-end exactly-once results, which is the property feature pipelines need.
body.heading: A stream as an unbounded table

body.body: Windowed aggregations group by event time taken from the record, not by arrival time. A watermark declares how late data may arrive, for example ten minutes behind the maximum event time seen; rows older than that are dropped and the state for closed windows is released. Without a watermark, state grows without bound and the job eventually fails. Stream-stream joins also need watermarks on both sides plus a time-range condition. Operating a streaming job means watching input rate against processing rate, batch duration, state store size and consumer lag.
body.heading: Event time, watermarks and state

subtopics.title: Structured Streaming for near-real-time features

body.body: A production batch job takes a logical date as a parameter, reads only the input partitions for that date, and overwrites only the matching output partition. With dynamic partition overwrite, or a transactional table format, a retry or a backfill produces the same result instead of duplicates. Jobs avoid collect on large data, avoid wall-clock time inside transformations, and write a controlled number of files per partition. Schema is declared explicitly so that an upstream change fails loudly at read time.
body.heading: Idempotent, partition-scoped writes

body.body: Spark runs on Kubernetes, YARN or a managed service; in each case the platform decides executor sizing, dynamic allocation, use of spot capacity for executors, and per-team quotas. Standard practice is a job template that fixes the Spark version, image, logging and metrics configuration, so teams only supply code and resource hints. Unit tests run transformations on a local SparkSession with small fixtures, and data quality checks on row counts, null rates and key uniqueness run as a step after the write and before downstream consumers are triggered.
body.heading: Platform concerns

subtopics.title: Running Spark jobs in production

concepts.summary: Apache Spark is the default engine for building training sets and feature tables that do not fit on one machine. A driver plans a query over DataFrames, splits it into stages and tasks, and executors run those tasks over partitions of data. The platform engineer's job is to make such jobs correct on rerun, predictable in cost, and operable on shared clusters.
concepts.title: Large-scale data pipelines with Spark and PySpark

  LH --> KV[Key-value online store]
  KV --> INF[Inference services]
  PG[PostgreSQL metadata store] --> TR
  PG --> REG[Registry and job state]
  CAT[Catalog and lineage] --- LH
  CAT --- WH

concepts.in_practice: A typical platform lands raw data in object storage, refines it with batch jobs into lakehouse or warehouse tables partitioned by date, and exposes curated tables to data scientists through SQL. Service state and ML metadata live in a managed PostgreSQL instance with time-partitioned tables for high-volume logs, and features needed at request time are pushed into DynamoDB or Redis. Platform engineers review table layouts when a table is created, enforce partition filters and expirations by default, publish cost per team, and run scheduled compaction and snapshot expiry. Store selection is written down per access pattern, because most later pain comes from serving point lookups out of an analytical store or analytics out of an operational one.

sources.title: Best practices for designing and architecting with DynamoDB

body.body: A data lake is columnar files, usually Parquet, in object storage, organized by directory partitions. It is cheap and scales without limit, but plain directories give no atomic commits, no safe concurrent writers and slow listing. Lakehouse table formats such as Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi add a metadata layer that records which files make up each table version. That brings ACID commits, schema evolution, time travel to an earlier snapshot, and file-level statistics that let engines skip data. For ML, snapshot identifiers make a training set reproducible: a run records the table version it read.
body.heading: Files plus a transaction log

body.body: Performance depends on file layout. Partition by a low-cardinality column that most queries filter on, typically date; over-partitioning produces millions of small files and slow planning. Compaction jobs merge small files toward a target size of some hundreds of megabytes, and clustering or sorting within files improves skipping on secondary filter columns. Old snapshots and unreferenced files must be expired on a schedule or storage grows forever. A catalog such as a Hive-compatible metastore, AWS Glue or Unity Catalog maps table names to locations and carries access control.
body.heading: Layout and maintenance

subtopics.title: Data lake and lakehouse table formats

body.body: In BigQuery a partitioned table is divided into segments by a time-unit column, ingestion time or an integer range; a query that filters on the partitioning column scans only matching partitions, and on-demand cost follows bytes scanned. Clustering sorts data within partitions by chosen columns so block-level pruning applies to further filters. Snowflake stores every table automatically in micro-partitions, contiguous units of compressed columnar storage with min and max metadata per column; pruning works when the data is well clustered on the filter columns, and a clustering key can be defined for very large tables whose natural load order does not match query filters.
body.heading: How pruning works in BigQuery and Snowflake

body.body: The practical levers are the same in both: always filter on the partition or clustering column, select only needed columns, and avoid wrapping the filter column in a function that defeats pruning. BigQuery can require a partition filter on a table and set partition expiration; dry runs report bytes that would be scanned before paying. In Snowflake, clustering depth indicates how well a table is clustered, and reclustering consumes credits, so keys are reserved for large tables with stable query patterns. Teams add per-team cost attribution through labels or tags and alert on unusually expensive queries.
body.heading: Keeping cost under control

subtopics.title: Warehouse partitioning, clustering and spend

body.body: Most ML platform control planes keep state in PostgreSQL: experiment runs, model registry entries, job status, labels. B-tree is the default index and serves equality and range queries; GIN indexes serve jsonb containment and full-text search; BRIN indexes are tiny and suit very large append-only tables correlated with time. Multicolumn and partial indexes should mirror real query predicates, and every index adds write cost. Declarative partitioning by range, list or hash splits a large table so the planner prunes partitions and old data is removed by detaching or dropping a partition instead of a slow bulk delete. Prefer jsonb over json for stored semi-structured metadata because it is indexable.
body.heading: Indexes, partitioning and JSONB

body.body: PostgreSQL uses multiversion concurrency control: each statement sees a snapshot, so readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers. The price is that updates and deletes leave dead row versions that vacuum must reclaim. Long-running transactions, such as an analytics query or an idle open session, hold back cleanup and cause table and index bloat. For platform services this means short transactions, connection pooling, monitoring of autovacuum and oldest transaction age, and sending heavy analytical reads to a replica or to the warehouse.
body.heading: MVCC consequences

subtopics.title: PostgreSQL as the operational and metadata store

body.body: Inference-time reads need single-digit millisecond lookups by entity key at high request rates, which is the job of a key-value store such as DynamoDB or Redis. DynamoDB design starts from the list of access patterns, not from a normalized schema: choose a partition key with high cardinality and even traffic so load spreads across partitions, add a sort key to group related items under one partition key, and use secondary indexes sparingly for the few alternate lookups. A hot partition key throttles regardless of total table capacity.
body.heading: Design from access patterns

body.body: Keep items small and store large payloads in object storage with a pointer. Use time-to-live attributes to expire stale feature rows, and batch reads to fetch several entities in one round trip. Choose on-demand capacity for spiky or unknown traffic and provisioned capacity with autoscaling for steady traffic. Bulk loads from batch pipelines should be rate-limited or use import features so they do not starve online reads. Redis gives lower latency and richer data types but is bounded by memory, so it suits small, hot feature sets and caches.
body.heading: Operational choices

subtopics.title: Key-value stores for online lookups

body.body: Owning storage means more than buckets and tables. Each dataset needs an owner, a schema, a freshness expectation, a sensitivity classification and lineage to the job that produced it, held in a catalog. Training sets are referenced by an immutable identifier, such as a table snapshot or a content hash, recorded with the model so results can be reproduced and audited. Lifecycle rules move cold objects to cheaper storage classes and expire raw data, intermediate outputs and old snapshots after a retention period. Deletion requests must propagate to derived tables, so lineage is a compliance tool as well as a debugging tool.
body.heading: What the platform must track

subtopics.title: Lifecycle, metadata and dataset versioning

concepts.summary: ML systems use several stores, each chosen for one access pattern: object storage and lakehouse tables for bulk training data, a warehouse for analytical SQL, a relational database for metadata and transactional state, and a key-value store for low-latency lookups at inference. The core skills are matching the store to the read pattern, laying data out so queries scan little, and managing lifecycle and spend as volume grows.
concepts.title: Storage for ML: lakehouse, warehouse and operational data stores

from datetime import timedelta
from feast import Entity, FeatureView, Field, FileSource
from feast.types import Float32, Int64

driver = Entity(name='driver', join_keys=['driver_id'])

source = FileSource(
    path='data/driver_stats.parquet',
    timestamp_field='event_timestamp',
)

driver_stats = FeatureView(
    name='driver_hourly_stats',
    entities=[driver],
    ttl=timedelta(days=1),
    schema=[Field(name='conv_rate', dtype=Float32),
            Field(name='avg_daily_trips', dtype=Int64)],
    source=source,
)

import pandas as pd
from feast import FeatureStore

store = FeatureStore(repo_path='.')
features = ['driver_hourly_stats:conv_rate',
            'driver_hourly_stats:avg_daily_trips']

# training: as-of join at each label timestamp
entity_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'driver_id': [1001, 1002],
    'event_timestamp': pd.to_datetime(['2026-01-05 10:00', '2026-01-06 09:30']),
})
train_df = store.get_historical_features(
    entity_df=entity_df, features=features).to_df()

# serving: latest values from the online store
online = store.get_online_features(
    features=features, entity_rows=[{'driver_id': 1001}]).to_dict()

concepts.in_practice: A team keeps feature definitions in a Git repository next to the pipelines that compute them; CI runs a plan against the registry and merges apply the change. Batch pipelines write timestamped feature tables to the offline store, an orchestrator task runs incremental materialization after each successful load, and a streaming job pushes the few features that need minute-level freshness. Data scientists build training sets by passing an entity dataframe with label timestamps to historical retrieval, and the serving code fetches the same feature service by name. The platform team owns the online store capacity, freshness alerts per feature view, access control on feature groups, and a periodic offline versus online consistency check.

body.body: The registry holds feature definitions as versioned metadata: which entities exist, which features belong to which view, where the source data lives. The offline store is a warehouse or lakehouse table set with full history, read in bulk to build training sets. The online store is a key-value database holding only the latest values per entity key, read at request time with low latency. Feast is an open-source implementation that plugs into existing stores instead of replacing them; it does not run the transformations that produce batch features, which stay in upstream pipelines. Amazon SageMaker Feature Store offers the same split as a managed service through feature groups with an online store, an offline store, or both.
body.heading: Three components and two read paths

body.body: The cost is another system to operate, so the case rests on reuse and correctness. It pays off when several models share features, when models serve online and need the same values that were used offline, and when training needs history joined at the correct time. A single batch-scored model with features computed in one SQL query usually does not need one. Platform teams often start with only the offline path and conventions for timestamped feature tables, then add online serving when the first real-time model arrives.
body.heading: When a feature store is worth it

subtopics.title: Architecture: registry, offline store, online store

body.body: In Feast, an entity is the business object features describe, identified by a join key such as a user id. A data source points to a table or file with an event timestamp column. A feature view groups a set of features over one source for one or more entities, with a schema and a time-to-live that bounds how far back a value may be used. A feature service names the exact set of features one model version consumes, which gives a stable contract between the model and the store. Definitions are Python files in a repository; running the apply command registers them and prepares the infrastructure.
body.heading: The definition objects

body.body: Some features cannot be precomputed because they depend on the request, for example the ratio between a transaction amount in the request and a stored average. On-demand feature views express such transformations so they run in both historical retrieval and online retrieval, keeping one definition. Features with tight freshness needs arrive from a stream processor that pushes values into the online store and logs them to the offline store. In SageMaker Feature Store the equivalent unit is a feature group, where every record carries a record identifier and an event time.
body.heading: On-demand and streaming features

subtopics.title: Defining entities, feature views and feature services

body.body: Historical retrieval takes an entity dataframe, one row per training example with entity keys and an event timestamp (usually the moment the label's prediction would have been made). For each row and each feature view, the store selects the most recent feature row whose timestamp is at or before the example timestamp and no older than the view's time-to-live; otherwise the feature is null. This as-of join is what prevents label leakage from future values. It is expensive on large tables, so offline stores implement it as a windowed SQL query, and teams keep feature tables partitioned by time to bound the scan.
body.heading: The join a feature store performs

subtopics.title: Point-in-time correct training sets

body.body: Materialization copies the latest feature values per entity from the offline store into the online store for a time range. An incremental materialize run processes only the interval since the previous run, and is scheduled from an orchestrator at the cadence the freshness requirement allows. Because the online store keeps one row per entity key per view, a rerun overwrites the same keys and is safe to retry. Failures here are silent for the model, which keeps serving stale values, so the platform tracks the last successful materialization time per view and alerts when it exceeds the expected interval.
body.heading: Loading the online store

body.body: At inference the model service requests features for a list of entity rows, either through the SDK in process or through a feature server over the network. Latency is dominated by the online store read, so features for one request are batched into a single call, feature services limit the fetch to what the model needs, and missing entities return nulls that the model must handle with defaults. Capacity planning treats the online store as a tier-one dependency of the model endpoint: it shares the endpoint's availability target, timeouts and fallbacks.
body.heading: Serving path

subtopics.title: Materialization and online retrieval

body.body: Skew is any difference between the feature values a model trained on and the values it receives in production. Common causes are two implementations of the same logic (SQL offline, application code online), different handling of nulls and defaults, timezone or window boundary differences, stale online values after a failed materialization, and backfills that use data which was not yet available at the original time. A feature store removes the first cause by having one definition and one retrieval interface for both paths, but freshness and backfill discipline remain the team's responsibility.
body.heading: Sources of skew

body.body: The strongest control is to log the features actually served with each prediction and train on those logs, or at least compare them with offline-computed values for the same entity and timestamp and track the mismatch rate per feature. Other controls are schema and range validation on feature tables before materialization, pinning a model version to a feature service version, and treating a feature definition change like an API change with review and a migration plan. Distribution monitoring on served features catches drift that tests cannot.
body.heading: Controls

subtopics.title: Detecting and preventing training-serving skew

concepts.summary: A feature store is the system that defines features once and serves the same values to training and to online inference. It pairs an offline store holding timestamped history with an online store holding the latest value per entity, plus a registry of definitions. Its main purpose is correctness: training rows must see only what was known at the time, and serving must compute features the same way training did.
concepts.title: Feature stores and feature pipelines: offline/online consistency

Each lesson starts from the architecture and then goes into the operating details a platform engineer owns, such as partitioning, cost, correctness over time and failure recovery.

concepts.in_practice: A typical ML platform team runs Airflow on Kubernetes from the official Helm chart or uses a managed offering, with DAGs delivered from a Git repository through CI. Data scientists get a template DAG with standard stages: validate inputs, build features, train, evaluate, register. Each heavy stage runs as a pod or an external job, and Airflow only tracks state and passes references such as a storage path or a model version. The team sets default retries, timeouts and failure callbacks through shared default arguments, uses pools to protect scarce resources such as GPUs and warehouse slots, and watches scheduler health, parse time and task queue latency. Retraining is scheduled by time or triggered by upstream data updates, and backfills are run with concurrency limits after feature logic changes.

body.body: A DAG is a Python-defined collection of tasks with directed dependencies and no cycles. It describes order and conditions of execution, not what the tasks do internally. A task is an instance of an operator (a prebuilt template such as a Bash, Python or Kubernetes pod operator), a sensor (waits for an external condition) or a function decorated with the TaskFlow task decorator. Dependencies are declared with the bitshift operators or set_upstream and set_downstream, and TaskFlow infers them from function calls. Each scheduled execution creates a DAG run, and each task in it becomes a task instance with its own state: queued, running, success, failed, up for retry or skipped.
body.heading: Core concepts

body.body: Beyond linear chains, Airflow supports branching (pick one downstream path at runtime), trigger rules (run a task when all upstream succeeded, when any failed, or always, which is useful for cleanup and alerts), task groups for visual and logical grouping, and dynamic task mapping, which expands one task into many instances at runtime from a list, for example one training task per region or hyperparameter set. Small values pass between tasks through XCom; anything large should be written to object storage and passed by reference.
body.heading: Control flow

subtopics.title: The DAG model: tasks, operators and dependencies

body.body: A DAG has a start date and a schedule, which can be a cron expression, a preset such as daily, a timedelta, a custom timetable, or a data-aware trigger that fires when an upstream dataset or asset is updated. Each run carries a logical date and a data interval describing the slice of data it is responsible for. A daily run typically processes the previous complete day, so the run for an interval starts after that interval ends. Tasks should read the interval from the runtime context or templates instead of calling the current time, so that a rerun months later processes the same slice.
body.heading: How runs are timed

body.body: With catchup enabled, the scheduler creates a run for every interval between the start date and now that has not yet run; disabled, it only schedules the latest. Backfill deliberately reruns a historical range, for example after fixing a feature bug that requires recomputing ninety days of features. Both only work safely when tasks are partitioned by interval and idempotent. Limits such as max active runs and pools keep a backfill from flooding a warehouse or a GPU queue.
body.heading: Catchup and backfill

subtopics.title: Scheduling, data intervals, catchup and backfill

body.body: Airflow's guidance is to treat each task like a database transaction: it either completes fully or leaves nothing partial behind, and rerunning it gives the same result. In practice that means writing to a partition keyed by the data interval and overwriting it (or using upsert and merge) instead of appending, never relying on local disk between tasks because tasks may run on different workers, and avoiding non-deterministic inputs such as the current time. Retries are set per task with a count, a delay and optional exponential backoff. Timeouts, SLA-style alerts and on-failure callbacks turn a silent stall into a page or a chat message. For ML, training tasks should checkpoint to remote storage so a retry resumes instead of restarting.
body.heading: Tasks as transactions

subtopics.title: Idempotent tasks, retries and failure handling

body.body: An Airflow deployment has a scheduler that decides what should run, a DAG processor that parses DAG files, a metadata database (usually Postgres) holding all state, a web UI and API server, and an executor that determines where tasks run. The local executor runs tasks as subprocesses beside the scheduler. The Celery executor distributes them to a fixed pool of workers through a broker. The Kubernetes executor launches one pod per task, giving isolation and scale to zero at the cost of pod startup latency.
body.heading: Components

body.body: Independent of the executor, the Kubernetes pod operator runs a task as a pod from any image with its own resource requests, node selectors and tolerations. This keeps ML dependencies and GPU requirements out of the Airflow image. Platform teams commonly keep Airflow workers light and delegate: submit a Spark job, start a training job on a cluster or managed service, then poll or use a deferrable operator, which releases the worker slot while waiting and resumes through the triggerer process.
body.heading: The pattern for ML

subtopics.title: Architecture and executors: running tasks on Kubernetes

body.body: DAG files are parsed repeatedly by the DAG processor, so top-level code must be fast. Do not query databases, call APIs or read Airflow Variables at module level, and move heavy imports inside task functions. Read Variables and Connections through templates or inside the task at runtime. Keep secrets in Connections or a secrets backend, not in code. Generate similar DAGs from configuration with care, since each generated DAG adds parse time and scheduler load.
body.heading: Keep parsing cheap

body.body: A baseline CI test loads every DAG file and fails on import errors or cycles. Unit tests cover the Python callables in isolation, and a single DAG can be executed locally with the test command or dag.test for a debug run without a scheduler. DAGs ship through Git: synced into the deployment or baked into the image, promoted across staging and production, with the Airflow version and provider packages pinned so upgrades are deliberate.
body.heading: Testing and delivery

subtopics.title: DAG authoring practices and testing

concepts.summary: Airflow models a pipeline as a DAG of tasks defined in Python, and a scheduler decides when each task runs based on a schedule, dependencies and state. For ML platforms it is usually the control plane that triggers heavy work elsewhere (Spark, Kubernetes pods, training services) rather than the place where the compute happens. Running it well depends on idempotent tasks, careful DAG authoring and an executor that fits the workload.
concepts.title: Orchestrating ML pipelines with Airflow

concepts.in_practice: A platform team usually picks one ML-native orchestrator and wraps it in a golden path: a project template, base images with pinned ML libraries, a CI job that builds step images and registers or deploys the pipeline, and defaults for resources, retries and artifact locations. Data scientists develop a pipeline locally on a sample, then run it remotely with full data and GPUs by changing configuration instead of code. Runs are parameterized and triggered by a schedule, an upstream data pipeline or a merge. The final steps evaluate the model against a gate and register it. The team watches cache hit rates, queue wait times for GPU steps and failed-run causes, and keeps tenants isolated with namespaces, quotas and per-team storage prefixes.

body.body: A general scheduler records whether a task succeeded. An ML-native orchestrator also records what each step consumed and produced: datasets, models, metrics, with types and storage locations. That enables three things. Lineage: for any model, find the exact data, code version and parameters that produced it. Caching: if a step's inputs and code are unchanged, reuse the previous output instead of recomputing, which matters when a step is hours of GPU time. Reproducibility: each step runs in a pinned container image with declared resources, so a run can be repeated later or on another cluster.
body.heading: Artifacts, not just task state

body.body: ML pipelines are often run on demand with parameters (an experiment, a retrain for one segment) rather than only on a clock. They fan out widely for hyperparameter sweeps or per-partition training, need per-step resources such as GPUs and large memory, and are authored by data scientists who want plain Python and a fast local loop. These orchestrators optimize for those needs.
body.heading: Workload shape

subtopics.title: What ML-native orchestration adds

body.body: Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) is a platform for building and deploying portable, scalable ML workflows on Kubernetes, and one component of the wider Kubeflow project, which also covers notebooks, training operators, tuning and model serving. With the KFP Python SDK, a component is a function or container with typed inputs and outputs, and a pipeline is a function that wires components together. The SDK compiles the pipeline to an intermediate representation in YAML, which is submitted to a KFP backend. Each component executes as its own container, and the backend stores runs, experiments, parameters and artifacts so runs can be compared in the UI.
body.heading: Model

body.body: The backend runs in the cluster with an API server, a workflow engine (Argo Workflows in the open source distribution), a metadata store and an object store for artifacts. Step caching, recurring runs, and per-step resource and node placement settings are built in. The cost is operational: the platform team owns upgrades, multi-user isolation through namespaces and profiles, and the image build path for components.
body.heading: Operating it

subtopics.title: Kubeflow Pipelines

body.body: Flyte is an open source, Kubernetes-native workflow orchestrator for data and ML. Tasks are strongly typed Python functions, each run in a container, and workflows compose tasks into a graph that is checked at registration time, so many wiring errors surface before anything runs. Registered tasks and workflows are immutable and versioned, and executions are grouped by project and domain (for example development, staging, production), giving a multi-tenant structure out of the box. Launch plans bind a workflow to default inputs, schedules and notifications.
body.heading: Model

body.body: Flyte passes typed data between tasks through object storage and tracks it, supports caching keyed on inputs and a cache version, dynamic workflows and map tasks for large fan-out, per-task resource requests including GPUs, and retries that can distinguish system failures such as spot preemption from user errors. Plugins hand a task to Spark, Ray or distributed training operators. It suits organizations that want strong contracts and a central platform serving many teams.
body.heading: Why teams pick it

subtopics.title: Flyte

body.body: Prefect turns ordinary Python into workflows with a flow decorator on the entry function and a task decorator on units of work. Control flow is native Python, so loops and conditionals work as written and the graph is discovered at runtime rather than declared up front. Tasks get retries, caching and concurrency controls, and state is reported to a Prefect server or the hosted cloud service. To run on a schedule or in response to events, a flow is packaged as a deployment and executed by workers pulling from a work pool backed by infrastructure such as Kubernetes or containers.
body.heading: Prefect

body.body: A Metaflow flow is a class deriving from FlowSpec; methods marked as steps are nodes, and each step calls self.next to name its successor. Any value assigned to self becomes a persisted, versioned artifact available in later steps and after the run through the client API. Branches and foreach fan out, and a join step merges results. The same code runs locally or with steps dispatched to cloud batch compute or Kubernetes through decorators that request resources, and flows can be deployed to a production scheduler.
body.heading: Metaflow

subtopics.title: Prefect and Metaflow

body.body: Start with who writes pipelines. Data scientists iterating on models favor Metaflow or Prefect for the local loop and low ceremony; a central platform with many tenants favors Flyte or KFP for typed interfaces, isolation and governance. Next, where compute lives: KFP and Flyte assume Kubernetes, Metaflow fits cloud batch services as well, and Prefect is infrastructure agnostic. Then consider operating cost, since KFP and Flyte are multi-service control planes that need an owner. Finally, check integration with the model registry, experiment tracker and feature store already in place.
body.heading: Decision factors

body.body: Many organizations run two layers: a general scheduler such as Airflow for data pipelines and cross-system coordination, and an ML-native tool for training and evaluation graphs, with the scheduler triggering ML pipeline runs through an API. Lower-level engines such as Argo Workflows sit underneath several of these tools and are sometimes used directly by platform teams for container-native DAGs.
body.heading: Coexistence

subtopics.title: Choosing and combining orchestrators

concepts.summary: ML-native orchestrators treat a pipeline as a graph of containerized, typed steps that produce versioned artifacts, rather than as scheduled tasks that happen to run ML code. Kubeflow Pipelines and Flyte are Kubernetes-native platforms; Prefect and Metaflow are Python-first frameworks that start on a laptop and scale out to remote compute. Choosing between them is mostly a question of who authors pipelines, where compute lives and how much platform the team wants to operate.
concepts.title: ML-native orchestrators: Kubeflow Pipelines, Flyte, Prefect and Metaflow

from datetime import timedelta
from temporalio import activity, workflow
from temporalio.common import RetryPolicy

@activity.defn
async def run_eval(model_id: str) -> float:
    return 0.93  # call the evaluation service here

@workflow.defn
class PromoteModel:
    @workflow.run
    async def run(self, model_id: str) -> str:
        score = await workflow.execute_activity(
            run_eval, model_id,
            start_to_close_timeout=timedelta(minutes=30),
            retry_policy=RetryPolicy(maximum_attempts=3))
        return "promote" if score > 0.9 else "reject"

concepts.in_practice: A team introduces Temporal for one process that keeps breaking under glue code, such as model promotion: a workflow runs an evaluation activity, waits for an approval signal with a timeout, calls activities that update the registry and trigger a canary rollout, watches metrics on a timer, and compensates by rolling back on failure. Workers run as Kubernetes deployments, split by task queue so slow or GPU-bound activities do not starve short ones, and autoscale on queue backlog. Activities are written to be idempotent with keys derived from workflow and activity ids, large inputs travel as storage references, and replay tests against recorded histories run in CI before each worker release. Consumers on the message broker translate events into workflow starts or signals keyed by a business id, and operators debug by reading event histories in the UI instead of correlating logs across services.

body.body: A workflow definition is ordinary code in a supported language. A workflow execution is one run of it, identified by a workflow id. As it progresses, the Temporal Service appends events to that execution's history: workflow started, activity scheduled, activity completed with its result, timer fired, signal received. If the worker process dies, another worker picks up the execution, re-runs the workflow function from the top and feeds it the recorded results instead of re-executing completed steps, until it reaches the point where it left off. The effect is that local variables and the call stack survive crashes, deployments and restarts, and a workflow can sleep for days or months while holding no compute.
body.heading: How it works

body.body: Without durable execution, the same guarantees require hand-built state machines, status tables, polling jobs, queues with redelivery and reconciliation scripts. Temporal moves that into the platform, leaving the business sequence readable as straight-line code.
body.heading: What it replaces

subtopics.title: Durable execution: workflows, event history and replay

body.body: Because replay re-executes workflow code against recorded history, the code must be deterministic: given the same history it must issue the same commands in the same order. Workflow code must not call the network, read files, use the system clock, generate random numbers or spawn threads directly. The SDK provides safe equivalents such as workflow time, timers, random and UUID helpers, and anything else belongs in an activity. A mismatch between code and history is raised as a non-determinism error.
body.heading: The rule

body.body: Executions may outlive several deployments, so changing the order or set of commands in workflow code can break in-flight runs. Teams handle this with patching or versioning APIs that branch on whether an execution started before the change, with worker versioning that pins executions to compatible builds, or by routing new starts to a new workflow type. Very long or looping workflows use continue-as-new to start a fresh execution with a clean history, and replay tests in CI run recorded histories against new code before release.
body.heading: Changing running workflows

subtopics.title: Determinism constraints and versioning workflow code

body.body: An activity is a normal function that performs a single well-defined action that may fail: calling a service, writing to a database, launching a training job. Activities are retried by default under a retry policy with initial interval, backoff coefficient, maximum interval, maximum attempts and a list of non-retryable error types. Timeouts bound them: start-to-close limits one attempt, schedule-to-close limits the total including retries, and a heartbeat timeout detects a stuck or dead worker when a long activity reports progress periodically. Heartbeats can carry details such as a checkpoint so the next attempt resumes. Execution is at-least-once, so activities should be idempotent, typically by passing an idempotency key derived from the workflow id and activity id to the downstream system.
body.heading: Beyond a hand-built job runtime

subtopics.title: Activities: retries, timeouts, heartbeats and idempotency

body.body: A running workflow can receive signals (asynchronous messages that are recorded in history and can change its course), answer queries (read-only inspection of current state), and handle updates (synchronous requests that are validated, change state and return a result). Workflows can wait on a condition with a timeout, which expresses patterns such as wait for human approval for up to three days and otherwise escalate. Child workflows and timers complete the toolkit, and the saga pattern is written as plain code: on failure, run compensating activities for steps already done.
body.heading: Message passing into workflows

body.body: In an event-driven architecture, a broker such as RabbitMQ or Kafka carries events between services, while Temporal owns the stateful process that reacts to them. A thin consumer turns each message into a workflow start or a signal-with-start addressed by a business key used as the workflow id, which also deduplicates redelivered messages. Activities publish outbound events. The broker gives fan-out and decoupling; the workflow gives ordering, timeouts and recovery per entity.
body.heading: Working with a message broker

subtopics.title: Signals, queries, updates and event-driven services

body.body: The Temporal Service (self-hosted with a database such as Postgres or Cassandra, or the hosted cloud offering) stores histories and dispatches tasks; it never runs application code. Workers are processes the team deploys that long-poll named task queues and execute workflow and activity code. Task queues are the routing and scaling unit: a GPU-bound activity can listen on its own queue served by workers on GPU nodes, while lightweight workflow workers scale separately. Namespaces isolate teams or environments, and the web UI and CLI show each execution's full history for debugging.
body.heading: Runtime topology

body.body: Good fits are model promotion with evaluation, approval and staged rollout steps; managing external training or fine-tuning jobs by start, poll and cleanup; batch inference campaigns; and long-running agent or data-remediation processes. Poor fits are data-heavy step graphs needing artifact lineage and caching, where ML-native orchestrators serve better. Payloads and histories have size limits, so pass references to object storage, not data.
body.heading: Fit and limits

subtopics.title: Workers, task queues and where Temporal fits in ML platforms

concepts.summary: Temporal provides durable execution: workflow code runs as if failures do not exist, because every step is recorded in an event history and the workflow can be rebuilt by replay after a crash. Side effects live in activities, which the platform retries and times out according to policy. On an ML platform it fits long-running, event-driven processes such as model promotion with human approval, fine-tuning job management and multi-step agent or data operations, more than scheduled batch DAGs.
concepts.title: Durable workflows and event-driven services with Temporal

modules.intro: Workflow orchestration is the layer that turns individual ML steps such as ingestion, feature computation, training, evaluation and deployment into repeatable, observable, retryable pipelines. This module covers the general-purpose scheduler most teams start with (Airflow), the ML-native orchestrators built around containers and artifacts, and durable execution with Temporal for long-running, event-driven processes.
modules.title: Workflow orchestration

import mlflow

concepts.in_practice: A platform team runs the tracking server as a small replicated deployment on Kubernetes in front of a managed PostgreSQL database and an object storage bucket, behind the company's single sign-on. Training job templates inject the tracking address and default tags as environment variables, and a shared helper library starts the run, turns on autologging and attaches the git commit and image digest. Experiments are named per team or project, old runs are pruned by a retention job, and database and bucket are backed up because losing tracking history means losing the lineage of every registered model. Teams that use Weights and Biases instead follow the same pattern with a hosted backend.

body.body: MLflow organises work into experiments, each holding many runs. A run is one execution of training code and carries four kinds of data. Parameters are key-value inputs such as learning rate or batch size, written once. Metrics are numeric values that can be logged repeatedly with a step and timestamp, which gives loss and accuracy curves. Tags are free-form metadata such as git commit, owner or dataset version. Artifacts are files of any size: model weights, plots, config files, evaluation reports. Every run has a unique run ID, a start and end time, and a status, and that ID is the handle everything downstream uses.
body.heading: What gets recorded

body.body: Parameters, metrics and tags are small and queryable, so they live in a database. Artifacts are large and opaque, so they live in object or file storage and the run only stores their location. This split drives the server architecture and the cost profile: metadata queries must be fast for the UI and search API, while artifact storage must be cheap and durable. Teams usually agree on a small set of mandatory tags so runs can be filtered consistently across projects.
body.heading: Why the split matters

subtopics.title: The tracking data model: experiments, runs, params, metrics, artifacts

body.body: A production MLflow deployment has three parts. The tracking server is a stateless HTTP service that exposes the REST API and the UI. The backend store is a SQL database, typically PostgreSQL or MySQL, holding experiments, runs, params, metrics and tags. The artifact store is object storage such as S3, GCS or Azure Blob. Clients can upload artifacts directly to the bucket with their own credentials, or the server can proxy artifact access so that clients only need to reach the server and never hold bucket credentials. Proxied access simplifies identity management but puts large uploads through the server, so it needs enough replicas and sensible timeouts.
body.heading: Two stores behind one server

subtopics.title: Tracking server architecture: backend store and artifact store

body.body: Explicit logging wraps training in a run context and calls log_param, log_metric and log_artifact where needed. It is precise but relies on every author remembering to do it. Autologging is switched on with a single call and hooks into supported frameworks such as PyTorch Lightning, scikit-learn, XGBoost and Keras to capture parameters, per-epoch metrics and the trained model without code changes. Platforms usually combine both: autologging for the baseline, plus a thin wrapper that adds mandatory tags like git commit, container image and dataset version. The client finds the server through the MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI environment variable, which the platform injects into every training pod so user code contains no addresses.
body.heading: Two ways to log

subtopics.title: Instrumenting training code: explicit logging and autologging

body.body: The value of tracking appears when runs are compared. The MLflow UI and the search API filter runs by parameter, metric or tag and plot metric curves side by side, which answers questions like which learning rate converged fastest. Reproducibility needs more than hyperparameters: the run should also record the source revision, the environment or image, the dataset version and the random seed. With those in place, a run ID becomes a complete recipe. The same ID then links forward into the model registry, so a model version in production can be traced back to the exact run, metrics and artifacts that produced it.
body.heading: From a list of runs to a decision

subtopics.title: Comparing runs and making results reproducible

concepts.summary: Experiment tracking records what was run, with which inputs, and what came out, so any model can be traced back to its code, data and hyperparameters. MLflow Tracking is the most common open-source implementation: a client API that logs runs, and a server that stores metadata and artifacts. For a platform engineer the job is mostly running that server reliably and making logging the default path for every training job.
concepts.title: Experiment tracking with MLflow
