concepts.in_practice: A platform team creates dedicated GPU node pools per instance type, taints them, and installs the GPU Operator with Helm through the same GitOps flow as every other cluster add-on. On managed clouds they decide whether to use the provider's GPU-ready node image with a preinstalled driver or let the operator manage the driver. DCGM exporter metrics for utilization, memory and temperature flow into Prometheus and feed dashboards and idle-GPU alerts. Interactive and small inference workloads go on time-sliced or MIG pools, training jobs get whole GPUs, and driver upgrades are rolled out pool by pool after a canary node passes the operator's validation.

body.body: Four layers must line up on every GPU node. The NVIDIA kernel driver talks to the hardware. The NVIDIA Container Toolkit configures the container runtime, such as containerd, so that a container can be started with the driver libraries and device files mounted in. The NVIDIA device plugin runs as a DaemonSet, registers with the kubelet through the device plugin gRPC API, and advertises the node's GPUs as the extended resource nvidia.com/gpu. Finally the kubelet reports that capacity to the API server, and the scheduler can place pods against it. When a pod is admitted, the kubelet asks the plugin which devices to allocate and the runtime injects them.
body.heading: From hardware to an extended resource

body.body: Most GPU node problems are a mismatch between layers: a driver version that does not support the CUDA version in the image, a runtime not configured to use the NVIDIA runtime, or a device plugin pod that is not running so the node shows zero allocatable GPUs. The first debugging steps are to check node allocatable resources, check the plugin and driver pods on that node, and run nvidia-smi inside a test container.
body.heading: Where it breaks

subtopics.title: The layers between a pod and a GPU

body.body: Installing the layers by hand on every node image does not scale, so the GPU Operator manages them as containers. It is installed with Helm and uses the operator pattern to deploy and reconcile: the driver, either as a container or by using a driver preinstalled in the node image, the Container Toolkit, the device plugin, GPU Feature Discovery which labels nodes with GPU model, memory and capabilities, the DCGM exporter for Prometheus metrics, and a validator that confirms a node is ready. A custom resource called ClusterPolicy holds the configuration. Node Feature Discovery detects which nodes have NVIDIA hardware, so the components land only there. Upgrading drivers becomes a controlled rollout rather than a node image rebuild.
body.heading: One operator, many components

subtopics.title: Automating the stack with the NVIDIA GPU Operator

body.body: A container asks for GPUs in its resource limits, for example nvidia.com/gpu set to 1. GPUs are whole-number resources and cannot be overcommitted: if a request is given it must equal the limit, and specifying only the limit is enough. A pod that needs a particular GPU type selects it with a node selector or node affinity against labels published by GPU Feature Discovery, such as the product name or memory size.
body.heading: Resource requests

body.body: GPU nodes are expensive, so clusters stop ordinary pods from landing on them. The node pool carries a taint, commonly keyed nvidia.com/gpu with effect NoSchedule, and only pods with a matching toleration are scheduled there. A toleration permits placement but does not attract the pod, so it is paired with a GPU request or node affinity. Together with separate node pools per GPU type, this keeps system workloads on cheap CPU nodes and lets the autoscaler scale GPU pools to zero when idle.
body.heading: Taints and tolerations

subtopics.title: Requesting GPUs and keeping GPU nodes for GPU work

body.body: A whole GPU per pod wastes capacity for notebooks and small inference services. Time-slicing lets the device plugin advertise each GPU as several replicas; workloads take turns on the device with no memory or fault isolation. MPS, the Multi-Process Service, lets processes run concurrently on one GPU with better throughput than time-slicing, with limited isolation. MIG, Multi-Instance GPU, is available on supported data center GPUs and partitions one card into hardware-isolated instances with dedicated memory and compute, which is the right choice for multi-tenant use. Training jobs normally still take whole GPUs.
body.heading: Three sharing mechanisms

body.body: The device plugin model can only count identical devices. Dynamic Resource Allocation is the newer Kubernetes API for richer requests. Drivers publish devices and their attributes in ResourceSlices, administrators define DeviceClasses, and workloads state what they need in a ResourceClaim, optionally generated from a ResourceClaimTemplate. The scheduler matches claims to devices using attribute selectors, so a pod can ask for a GPU with a minimum amount of memory, or several containers can share one claimed device.
body.heading: Dynamic Resource Allocation

subtopics.title: Sharing GPUs: time-slicing, MPS, MIG and Dynamic Resource Allocation

concepts.summary: Kubernetes does not understand GPUs natively; it learns about them through a device plugin that advertises them as an extended resource. The NVIDIA stack supplies the pieces that make this work: kernel driver, container toolkit, device plugin and monitoring, usually installed together by the GPU Operator. This lesson covers how those layers fit, how pods request GPUs, and how a GPU can be shared or partitioned.
concepts.title: GPU compute on Kubernetes with the NVIDIA stack

code.code:
import torch, torch.nn as nn
import ray.train
from ray.train import ScalingConfig
from ray.train.torch import TorchTrainer, prepare_model

def train_loop_per_worker(config):
    model = prepare_model(nn.Linear(10, 1))  # wraps in DDP, moves to GPU
    opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=config["lr"])
    device = ray.train.torch.get_device()
    for epoch in range(config["epochs"]):
        x = torch.randn(64, 10, device=device)
        loss = model(x).pow(2).mean()
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        ray.train.report({"epoch": epoch, "loss": loss.item()})

trainer = TorchTrainer(
    train_loop_per_worker,
    train_loop_config={"lr": 0.01, "epochs": 3},
    scaling_config=ScalingConfig(num_workers=4, use_gpu=True),
)
result = trainer.fit()

concepts.in_practice: Teams start by making a training script work on one GPU, then on several GPUs in one node, and only then across nodes, measuring throughput at each step to see whether scaling is worth the cost. The platform provides a blessed launch path, either a Ray cluster template or a set of Kubeflow training runtimes, with base images that pin compatible CUDA, driver and framework versions. Jobs write checkpoints to object storage, log metrics to the experiment tracker from the rank zero worker only, and are submitted through a queue so the whole worker group is admitted together. GPU utilisation and data loader wait time are watched on dashboards because a starved input pipeline is the most common reason added GPUs do not help.

body.body: The dominant pattern is data parallelism. Each worker process holds a full copy of the model on its own GPU and receives a different shard of every batch. After the backward pass, gradients are averaged across all workers with a collective all-reduce operation, so every copy applies the same update. In PyTorch this is DistributedDataParallel: each process has a rank, the group has a world size, and communication goes through a backend such as NCCL over the node network. A distributed sampler ensures workers see disjoint data. The effective batch size grows with the number of workers, which often means the learning rate has to be scaled too.
body.heading: Workers, ranks and gradient sync

body.body: Speedup is rarely linear. Gradient synchronisation costs network bandwidth, so interconnect speed between nodes matters, and one slow worker holds back the whole group because each step waits for everyone. Data loading is the other common bottleneck: if CPU workers or storage cannot feed the GPUs, utilisation drops no matter how many GPUs are added. Models too large for one GPU's memory need additional techniques such as sharding parameters or optimizer state across devices.
body.heading: What limits scaling

subtopics.title: How data-parallel training works

body.body: Ray Train wraps an existing training loop with little change. The user writes a per-worker training function and passes it to a trainer such as TorchTrainer along with a ScalingConfig that states the number of workers and whether each uses a GPU. Ray starts that many worker processes across the cluster, sets up the distributed process group, and runs the function on each. Helper calls prepare the model and data loader for distributed use, moving them to the right device and adding the sampler. Inside the loop the function reports metrics and checkpoints back to the driver. It has integrations for PyTorch, Lightning, Hugging Face Transformers, TensorFlow and XGBoost. On Kubernetes, Ray clusters are usually managed by the KubeRay operator.
body.heading: Trainer, scaling config, training function

subtopics.title: Ray Train: scaling a training loop from Python

body.body: Kubeflow Trainer is the Kubernetes-native approach. A platform team defines reusable runtimes, as ClusterTrainingRuntime or namespaced TrainingRuntime objects, that describe how a framework is launched: images, the number and roles of nodes, and the startup policy. Users submit a TrainJob that references a runtime and supplies their code, arguments and resource needs, either as YAML or through the Python SDK without writing manifests. The controller creates the group of pods, gives them stable network identities so workers can discover each other, and injects the environment the framework needs. It supports PyTorch, MPI-based workloads and others, and it is the successor to the older Training Operator with its per-framework resources such as PyTorchJob.
body.heading: TrainJob and runtimes

body.body: The split between runtime and job mirrors the split between platform and data science teams. Platform engineers own runtimes, base images, node selection and integration with a queueing system such as Kueue. Model developers only choose a runtime, a node count and resources per node. That keeps infrastructure detail out of user code and lets the platform change it centrally.
body.heading: Separation of concerns

subtopics.title: Kubeflow Trainer: distributed training as a Kubernetes resource

body.body: A multi-node job that runs for hours or days will see failures: a node is reclaimed, a GPU errors, a pod is preempted. Because all workers move in lockstep, losing one normally stops the whole group. The defence is periodic checkpointing of model weights, optimizer state, scheduler state and the current step to shared durable storage, usually object storage or a shared filesystem, written by one worker to avoid races. On restart the job loads the latest checkpoint and resumes. Ray Train can restart failed workers and restore from the last reported checkpoint up to a configured failure limit; on Kubernetes the job controller's restart policy does the same. Checkpoint frequency trades lost work against write overhead.
body.heading: Surviving worker loss

subtopics.title: Checkpointing and fault tolerance

concepts.summary: When a model or dataset is too large for one GPU, training is spread across several GPUs and several nodes that must start together, find each other and stay in sync. The training framework handles gradient synchronisation; the platform handles launching the worker group, wiring up networking and recovering from failures. Ray Train and Kubeflow Trainer are the two common ways to run this on Kubernetes.
concepts.title: Distributed training across multiple GPU nodes

flowchart LR
  J[Job created suspended with queue label] --> LQ[LocalQueue in team namespace]
  LQ --> CQ[ClusterQueue with quota per ResourceFlavor]
  CQ <-->|borrow and lend| CO[Cohort of ClusterQueues]
  CQ -->|quota available: admit and unsuspend| JC[Job controller creates pods]
  JC --> KS[kube-scheduler filters and scores nodes]
  KS --> N[GPU nodes]
  CQ -->|no quota: wait or preempt lower priority| LQ

concepts.in_practice: A platform team gives each group a LocalQueue backed by a ClusterQueue with a guaranteed GPU quota, places all queues in one cohort so idle capacity is borrowed, and defines a few priority classes such as production retraining, research and best-effort. Training job templates are created suspended with the queue label already set, and multi-worker jobs use all-or-nothing admission. Capacity planning runs on a regular cadence from metrics: pending time per queue, GPU allocation versus actual utilisation, and fragmentation across node types. Operations work includes cordoning and draining nodes for driver upgrades, handling failing GPUs, running reserved and spot capacity as separate flavors, and reviewing quota with team leads when wait times grow.

body.body: The Kubernetes scheduler watches for pods with no node assigned and places them one at a time. In the filtering phase it removes nodes that cannot run the pod because of insufficient resources, taints, affinity rules or other constraints. In the scoring phase it ranks the remaining feasible nodes and picks the highest, then binds the pod. This design is built for long-running services and works well for them. Its behaviour is extensible through scheduling framework plugins and profiles.
body.heading: Filter, score, bind

body.body: Three things are missing for batch. There is no job queue: a pod that does not fit simply stays pending, with no fair ordering between teams. There is no group awareness: a four-worker training job can get three pods placed and one stuck, holding three GPUs idle. And quota is a hard namespace cap through ResourceQuota, with no way to lend unused capacity to another team and take it back. Batch schedulers exist to fill these gaps.
body.heading: The gaps for training workloads

subtopics.title: What kube-scheduler does and where it falls short for batch

body.body: Kueue does not replace the scheduler. It decides when a job is allowed to start, then lets kube-scheduler place the pods. Jobs are created suspended; Kueue unsuspends them once quota is available. The main objects are the ResourceFlavor, which describes a kind of capacity such as a GPU model or spot versus on-demand nodes; the ClusterQueue, which holds quota per flavor and resource and the queueing and preemption policy; and the LocalQueue, a namespaced entry point that a team's jobs point to with a label. It works with batch Jobs, JobSet, Kubeflow jobs, Ray jobs and others.
body.heading: Admission instead of placement

body.body: ClusterQueues can be grouped in a cohort. A queue with unused nominal quota lends it to others in the cohort, and a queue under pressure can borrow up to a configured limit. When the owner needs its capacity back, preemption evicts borrowing workloads according to priority. This gives each team a guaranteed share while keeping GPUs busy. Workload priority classes decide ordering within a queue, and admission can be made all-or-nothing so a job starts only when every pod can be admitted.
body.heading: Borrowing and preemption

subtopics.title: Kueue: job queueing, quotas and fair sharing

body.body: Gang scheduling means a group of pods is scheduled only if a minimum number of them can run at the same time. This is what distributed training and MPI jobs require, since a partial group does no useful work and wastes the GPUs it holds. Volcano is a batch scheduler for Kubernetes that implements this with a PodGroup object carrying a minimum member count. It runs as an additional scheduler that pods opt into by scheduler name, and it adds its own queues with weights and capacity, fair-share and priority policies, preemption and reclaim between queues, and bin-packing style placement that reduces GPU fragmentation. It integrates with frameworks such as Spark, PyTorch, TensorFlow, MPI and Ray. The choice between Volcano and Kueue often comes down to whether a team wants to replace placement logic or only add admission control on top of the default scheduler.
body.heading: All or nothing placement

subtopics.title: Gang scheduling and Volcano

body.body: Many large GPU clusters run Slurm rather than Kubernetes. A central controller daemon, slurmctld, tracks resources and the job queue, and a slurmd daemon on each compute node launches work. Nodes are grouped into partitions, which act as queues with their own limits. Users interact through a small set of commands: sbatch submits a batch script for later execution, srun launches a job or a step interactively, salloc reserves an allocation, squeue lists queued and running jobs, sinfo shows partition and node state, and scancel removes a job. A job requests nodes, tasks, GPUs and a time limit, waits until the allocation is available, then runs on bare metal with direct access to the hardware and interconnect.
body.heading: Daemons, partitions and commands

body.body: Slurm treats a multi-node job as a single unit by default, so gang scheduling is inherent, and time limits let it backfill short jobs into gaps. Kubernetes offers stronger isolation through containers, a richer API and better fit for services. Platform teams increasingly need both mental models.
body.heading: How it compares

subtopics.title: Slurm: the HPC scheduling model

concepts.summary: A shared GPU cluster has more demand than capacity, so something must decide which jobs run, in what order, and on whose budget. The default Kubernetes scheduler places individual pods but has no notion of queues, team quotas or all-or-nothing job groups. Batch systems such as Kueue and Volcano add those on Kubernetes, while Slurm is the long-established scheduler on HPC-style clusters.
concepts.title: Workload scheduling, capacity management and GPU cluster operations

modules.intro: Training infrastructure is the part of an ML platform that turns expensive GPU hardware into repeatable, traceable training runs. This module covers how runs are recorded, how GPUs are exposed to Kubernetes, how one job spans many nodes, and how a shared cluster decides who runs when.
modules.title: Training infrastructure

import mlflow
from mlflow import MlflowClient
from mlflow.models import infer_signature

with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    sig = infer_signature(X_train, model.predict(X_train))
    info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(
        model, name="model", signature=sig,
        registered_model_name="fraud-scorer",
    )

client = MlflowClient()
v = info.registered_model_version
client.set_model_version_tag("fraud-scorer", v, "git_sha", GIT_SHA)
client.set_model_version_tag("fraud-scorer", v, "image_digest", IMAGE_DIGEST)

concepts.in_practice: A training pipeline finishes by logging the model in a standard format with its signature and registering it as a new version, tagged with the commit, data snapshot and image digest. Automated evaluation writes its results onto the version, and an approver or a gate job flips the approval status or moves an alias. Deployment tooling only ever reads approved versions by alias or explicit version number, and production credentials can read the registry but training jobs cannot write to the production alias. The platform team owns naming conventions, required tags and retention rules, and enforces them in the registration step so that no unregistered artifact can reach serving.

sources.title: Model Registration Deployment with Model Registry (SageMaker)

body.body: A registry holds named models, and under each name an ordered list of versions. A version is immutable: it points to one artifact location and records the training run, parameters, metrics, code revision and data references that produced it. In MLflow this is a registered model with model versions linked to a tracking run; in SageMaker it is a Model Package Group containing versioned model packages. The registry does not replace the artifact store; it is a metadata index over it. Its value is that every other system, such as CI, deployment tooling and monitoring, can ask the same question and get the same answer: which exact version is this, where did it come from, and is it approved.
body.heading: Registered models, versions and lineage

subtopics.title: What a registry stores and why

body.body: An MLflow Model is a directory with an MLmodel descriptor file plus the serialized weights and environment files. The descriptor lists flavors, which are the ways the model can be loaded: a native flavor such as sklearn, pytorch or transformers, and usually the generic python_function flavor that exposes a uniform predict interface. It also carries a signature describing input and output schema, and optionally an input example. Dependency files pin the Python packages needed to load it. Because the format is self-describing, a serving layer or batch job can load any model the same way and validate requests against the signature before inference.
body.heading: The MLflow Model layout

body.body: For serving, the model directory is usually combined with a container image that holds the runtime, inference server and system libraries. Teams either bake weights into the image for small models or have the container pull the artifact at startup by registry reference for large ones. Either way the release unit is the pair of model version and image, and both must be recorded.
body.heading: Packaging beyond the artifact

subtopics.title: Packaging: a self-describing model artifact

body.body: Versions never change, so promotion is expressed with mutable pointers. MLflow uses aliases, named references such as champion or challenger that point at one version of a registered model and can be reassigned, plus free-form tags for annotations such as validation status. Deployment code resolves the alias instead of hard-coding a version number, so promoting a model is one atomic metadata update and rollback is moving the alias back. Many teams also separate environments by using distinct registered models or catalogs per environment and copying an approved version from the dev registry to the prod one, which keeps production access controls strict.
body.heading: Mutable pointers over immutable versions

body.body: SageMaker Model Registry attaches an approval status to each model package version: pending manual approval, approved or rejected. A status change emits an event that can trigger a deployment pipeline, which makes the human or automated approval the explicit boundary between training and release.
body.heading: Approval status

subtopics.title: Aliases, tags and promotion between environments

body.body: A model version is only reproducible if everything it depends on is pinned as well. Serving and training images should be referenced by digest, not by a floating tag, and the digest stored as metadata on the model version. Weights in object storage should sit under a versioned or content-hashed path with overwrites disabled, so the registry entry cannot silently point at different bytes. Recording the hash of the training data snapshot and the code commit closes the loop: given a model version, the platform can name the exact image, weights, code and data behind it, and an audit or a rollback does not depend on anyone's memory.
body.heading: Content addressing for the full release unit

subtopics.title: Pinning images and artifacts immutably

concepts.summary: A model registry is the system of record between training and serving: it gives each trained artifact a name, an immutable version, lineage back to the run that produced it, and a state that says whether it may be deployed. Packaging standardizes what an artifact contains so any serving stack can load it without knowing how it was trained. Together they make a release a reference to a specific, reproducible version instead of a file somebody copied.
concepts.title: Model registry, packaging and versioning

code.code:
import sys
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, recall_score

MAX_REGRESSION = 0.005   # allowed drop vs champion
MIN_SLICE_RECALL = 0.80

def gate(y, cand, champ, slices, threshold=0.5):
    failures = []
    ap_c, ap_b = average_precision_score(y, cand), average_precision_score(y, champ)
    if ap_c < ap_b - MAX_REGRESSION:
        failures.append(f"AP {ap_c:.4f} below champion {ap_b:.4f}")
    for name, mask in slices.items():
        r = recall_score(y[mask], cand[mask] >= threshold)
        if r < MIN_SLICE_RECALL:
            failures.append(f"slice {name} recall {r:.3f}")
    return failures

failures = gate(y_test, cand_scores, champ_scores, slice_masks)
if failures:
    sys.exit("GATE FAILED: " + "; ".join(failures))

concepts.in_practice: Teams run the gate as a pipeline step triggered by registration of a new version. The job loads the candidate and the current champion from the registry, evaluates both on pinned evaluation datasets, computes slice metrics and behavioral test failure rates, runs a short load test of the packaged model, and compares the results against thresholds kept in version control next to the pipeline. Results are logged to the tracking system and summarized on the model version; a failure blocks promotion and posts the diff to the owning team. Threshold changes go through code review, and a small set of overrides with a named approver exists for cases where a tradeoff is intentional.

sources.title: The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness
Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList

body.body: The metric must reflect how predictions are used. For classification, accuracy hides class imbalance, so teams look at precision, recall, F1, ROC AUC or average precision, and at calibration measures such as log loss or Brier score when the score itself is consumed as a probability. Threshold-dependent metrics need the operating threshold fixed as part of the release. For regression, mean absolute error, root mean squared error and R2 weigh large errors differently. Ranking and retrieval use metrics such as NDCG. scikit-learn exposes these as metric functions and as named scorers usable in cross-validation, which keeps offline evaluation consistent between experimentation and the gate.
body.heading: Metric families

body.body: A gate usually has one primary metric that must improve or hold, plus guardrails that must not regress: per-slice quality, fairness measures, inference latency, model size and memory footprint.
body.heading: Guardrail metrics

subtopics.title: Choosing metrics that match the decision

body.body: A regression suite evaluates every candidate on the same versioned datasets and compares it with the current production model evaluated on those same datasets in the same job, never against a number copied from an old report. The suite reports aggregate metrics and metrics per slice, such as region, device, customer tier or rare class, because an overall gain often hides a loss on a segment that matters. Thresholds are written as absolute floors and as maximum allowed regressions relative to the baseline. Since the test set is a sample, the comparison should include confidence intervals or a bootstrap so the gate does not flip on noise. The evaluation set must be kept out of training and refreshed on a schedule, otherwise repeated gating slowly overfits to it.
body.heading: Comparing candidate against champion

subtopics.title: Regression suites: frozen data, slices and baselines

body.body: Held-out accuracy overestimates real quality because the test set shares the biases of the training set. Behavioral testing treats the model as a black box and tests capabilities with three test types. A minimum functionality test is a small targeted set of simple cases for one capability, similar to a unit test. An invariance test applies perturbations that should not change the prediction, such as swapping a name or adding a typo, and fails if the output changes. A directional expectation test applies a change that should move the prediction in a known direction. Tests are generated at scale from templates, and failure rates per capability become additional gate criteria alongside the aggregate metrics.
body.heading: The CheckList approach

subtopics.title: Behavioral testing beyond held-out accuracy

body.body: The ML Test Score rubric groups production readiness checks into four areas: tests for features and data, tests for model development, tests for ML infrastructure, and monitoring tests. Examples include verifying that feature distributions match expectations, that the model beats a simple baseline, that training is reproducible, that the full pipeline has an integration test, that a model can be rolled back, and that serving and training compute features the same way. For a platform engineer the lesson is that a release gate should include non-model checks: schema and signature compatibility with the serving contract, a load test against the latency budget, and a smoke test of the packaged artifact in the real serving image.
body.heading: The ML Test Score view

body.body: The gate writes metrics, thresholds, dataset versions and pass or fail onto the model version in the registry, so promotion tooling can refuse anything without a passing record.
body.heading: Recording the verdict

subtopics.title: Gating the whole system, not only the model

concepts.summary: An evaluation gate turns the question of whether a model is good enough into an automated, repeatable check that blocks promotion when it fails. It combines the right metrics for the task, a fixed regression suite compared against the current production model, behavioral tests for specific capabilities, and checks on the surrounding system such as latency and data assumptions. The output is a recorded verdict attached to the model version.
concepts.title: Model evaluation: regression suites and release gates

concepts.in_practice: A platform team publishes a small set of reusable workflows: one that builds and scans an image and outputs its digest, one that submits a training pipeline, one that runs the evaluation gate against a registry version, and one that promotes a version by opening a pull request on the deployment repository. Model teams call these from a short workflow in their own repository and supply only parameters. Production promotion sits behind a protected environment with required reviewers, deploy jobs use a concurrency group per environment, and all cloud access goes through short-lived federated roles. Long-running work is delegated to the orchestrator, with the workflow recording run links and identifiers in the job summary.

sources.title: MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning

body.body: A workflow is a YAML file under the repository's workflows directory. The on key names triggering events such as push, pull_request, schedule or workflow_dispatch. Jobs run in parallel by default on a runner chosen by runs-on, and are ordered with needs. Each job is a list of steps that either run shell commands or use a packaged action. For platform work the important features are reusable workflows invoked through workflow_call, matrix strategies, concurrency groups that prevent overlapping deploys, and job outputs that pass an image digest or model version to later jobs.
body.heading: Events, jobs, steps and runners

subtopics.title: Workflow anatomy

body.body: In an ML system, CI tests and validates not only code but also data schemas and models; CD delivers a training pipeline that in turn delivers a prediction service; and continuous training automatically retrains and serves models when triggered by new data, a schedule or detected performance decay. A widely used maturity model describes three levels. At level 0 everything is manual and script driven, with rare releases. At level 1 the training pipeline is automated so models retrain continuously, with data validation and model validation as pipeline steps. At level 2 the pipeline itself has automated CI/CD, so changes to pipeline components are built, tested and deployed quickly and reliably.
body.heading: Three loops and maturity levels

body.body: A code change triggers CI on the pipeline code and images. A data or schedule trigger runs the deployed training pipeline. A newly approved model version triggers the serving deployment. Keeping these triggers separate avoids retraining on every commit.
body.heading: What triggers what

subtopics.title: CI, CD and continuous training for ML

body.body: A typical pipeline has a fast pull request stage: lint, unit tests for feature and preprocessing code, a tiny training smoke run on sample data, and a build of the training and serving images. After merge, images are pushed by digest and the training pipeline is submitted to the orchestrator or cluster; GitHub Actions launches and watches it but does not run long GPU training on a hosted runner. When training registers a new version, a gate job runs the evaluation suite. A passing version is promoted, and the deployment job opens a change against the environment configuration or calls the serving platform, which then performs the staged rollout. Each stage hands the next one explicit identifiers: commit, image digest, model version.
body.heading: Stages from commit to promotion

subtopics.title: Shape of a model release pipeline

body.body: Hosted runners suit linting, tests and image builds. Jobs that need GPUs, private network access or large caches run on self-hosted runners, commonly autoscaled on Kubernetes, and these must be isolated from untrusted pull requests. Cloud credentials should be short lived: the workflow requests an identity token and exchanges it for a cloud role scoped to that repository and branch, so no long-lived keys sit in secrets. Environments model deployment targets such as staging and production; they hold environment-scoped secrets and protection rules such as required reviewers, which gives a manual approval step before production. The permissions key should restrict the default token to the minimum, and third-party actions should be pinned to a commit.
body.heading: Securing and scaling the pipeline

subtopics.title: Runners, credentials and protected environments

concepts.summary: CI/CD for machine learning extends ordinary software delivery with two extra artifacts, data and models, and a third loop, continuous training. GitHub Actions is a common engine for it: workflows defined as YAML in the repository react to events, run jobs on runners, and call out to training, evaluation, registry and deployment systems. The platform engineer's job is to design the pipeline shape and the reusable building blocks that every model team shares.
concepts.title: CI/CD for models and services with GitHub Actions

concepts.in_practice: Teams keep an infrastructure repository with Terraform modules and per-environment root configurations, applied by CI after a reviewed plan, and a separate deployment repository with Kustomize overlays or Helm values per environment. Terraform creates the cluster and installs Argo CD, which then manages a root application that pulls in platform add-ons and an ApplicationSet that generates one application per model service and environment. Staging syncs automatically with prune and self-heal; production either syncs automatically from a protected branch or requires a manual sync. The release pipeline's last step is a bot pull request updating the model version and image digest, and anyone can answer what is running by reading Git.

body.body: Argo CD is a declarative continuous delivery controller for Kubernetes. Its central object is the Application, which binds a source, meaning a Git repository, revision and path containing manifests, Helm charts or Kustomize overlays, to a destination cluster and namespace. The target state is what Git declares; the live state is what is running. Sync status says whether the two match, and health status says whether the live resources are working. A sync applies the target state to the cluster. An AppProject groups applications and restricts which repositories, clusters and resource kinds they may use. Because the controller pulls from Git, CI systems never need cluster credentials; they only write to a repository.
body.heading: Target state, live state and sync

subtopics.title: The GitOps model and Argo CD concepts

body.body: With manual sync, Argo CD reports that an application is out of sync and waits for an operator. With an automated sync policy it applies changes as soon as Git changes. Two options matter operationally: prune deletes resources that were removed from Git, and self-heal reverts manual changes made directly in the cluster. Enabling both makes Git the only way to change the environment, which is the point, but it requires that emergency procedures also go through Git. Sync waves and hooks order resources, for example installing CRDs and running a migration job before workloads.
body.heading: Automated sync, prune and self-heal

body.body: Platform teams avoid hand-written Application objects. The app-of-apps pattern has one root application that manages other applications, and ApplicationSet generates applications from a template over a list of clusters, directories or repositories, which suits one inference service per model per environment.
body.heading: Scaling to many teams and clusters

subtopics.title: Sync policies, drift and managing many applications

body.body: Terraform's write, plan, apply cycle depends on state, the record that maps configuration to real resource identifiers and stores metadata such as dependencies. For a shared platform the state lives in a remote backend with locking so two applies cannot run at once, is split per environment and per layer to limit blast radius, and is treated as sensitive because it can contain secret values. For ML platforms the layers typically cover network, cluster and GPU node groups, object storage, registries and identity roles.
body.heading: State as the mapping to real resources

subtopics.title: Terraform workflow and state

body.body: A common split is that Terraform owns things with a cloud API and a slow change rate: accounts, networking, the cluster, node pools, buckets, registries, identity roles, and the initial installation of Argo CD itself. Argo CD owns everything inside the cluster: platform add-ons such as GPU operators, ingress and monitoring, and the workloads. Managing in-cluster Helm releases through Terraform works but couples every chart upgrade to a plan and apply and gives no continuous drift correction, so teams usually bootstrap Argo CD once and hand over.
body.heading: Splitting ownership cleanly

body.body: The serving manifest for a model references a model version or storage path and an image digest. Promotion is a pull request that changes those values in the environment overlay; Argo CD detects the commit and syncs it, and rollback is a revert of that commit. The registry remains the source of truth for what is approved, and Git records what is deployed where.
body.heading: A model release as a Git change

subtopics.title: Where Terraform stops and GitOps starts

concepts.summary: Reproducible environments come from declaring everything in version control and letting automation converge real systems toward it. Terraform declares cloud infrastructure and tracks it in state; Argo CD runs inside Kubernetes and continuously reconciles cluster resources against manifests in Git. For model releases this means a deployed model version is a line in a Git repository, with review, history and revert for free.
concepts.title: Reproducible environments: GitOps with Argo CD and infrastructure as code with Terraform

flowchart TD
  A[Approved model version] --> B[Shadow: mirrored traffic, responses discarded]
  B --> C{Latency, errors, diffs OK?}
  C -- no --> X[Stop and investigate]
  C -- yes --> D[Canary 5 percent]
  D --> E[Automated analysis]
  E -- fail --> R[Abort: traffic back to stable]
  E -- pass --> F[Canary 25 then 50 percent]
  F --> G[Full traffic]
  G --> H[Bake period with old version kept]
  H -- alarm --> R
  H -- clean --> I[Retire old version]

concepts.in_practice: A common sequence for a risky model change is shadow first for a day or more to compare latency, errors and prediction differences, then a canary at a few percent with automated analysis on service and model metrics, stepping up through pauses to full traffic, with the old version kept warm through a bake period. Low-risk refreshes skip shadow and go straight to canary. The platform team provides the rollout template, standard analysis queries and alarm definitions so model teams only set thresholds, and rollback is practiced regularly in staging. Champion/challenger tests are run through the experimentation system on top of the same routing, with the model version logged on every prediction.

body.body: In a shadow deployment the candidate runs next to the production model and receives a copy of live requests, but only the production model's response is returned to the caller. The shadow's outputs and operational metrics are logged for comparison. This validates things offline tests cannot: latency and error rate under real load, memory behavior, feature availability in the serving path, and how often predictions differ from the current model. SageMaker implements this as a shadow variant on an endpoint that receives a configured percentage of the production variant's requests, with a dashboard comparing the two, and service meshes offer the same idea as traffic mirroring. Limits: it doubles inference cost for the mirrored share, it must not trigger side effects twice, and it cannot measure outcomes that depend on users seeing the prediction.
body.heading: Real requests, discarded responses

subtopics.title: Shadow deployments

body.body: Argo Rollouts adds a Rollout resource that replaces a Deployment and manages ReplicaSets with progressive strategies. A canary strategy is a list of steps: set the canary weight to a percentage, pause for a duration or indefinitely until promoted, then continue. Without a traffic provider the weight is approximated by the ratio of canary to stable pods; with an ingress controller or service mesh integration the controller sets exact traffic percentages independently of replica counts, which matters for GPU services where each replica is expensive.
body.heading: Rollout resource, steps and traffic routing

body.body: An AnalysisTemplate defines metric queries, for example error rate or tail latency from Prometheus, with success conditions and failure limits. Analysis runs in the background or as a step during the rollout; if it fails, the controller aborts and shifts traffic back to the stable version. For models, add prediction-level signals such as score distribution or fallback rate, not only HTTP health.
body.heading: Automated analysis

subtopics.title: Canary releases with Argo Rollouts

body.body: Blue/green provisions the new version as a complete second fleet, tests it, then switches traffic, keeping the old fleet alive for a while so rollback is instant. It costs double capacity during the release but avoids running mixed versions under partial load. SageMaker deployment guardrails apply this to endpoint updates: a new fleet is created and traffic moves all at once, as a canary where a small portion shifts first and the rest follows after a baking period, or linearly in equal steps. CloudWatch alarms are attached to the deployment, and if any alarm trips during a baking period the service automatically rolls traffic back to the old fleet. A rolling option updates the fleet in batches when doubling capacity is not acceptable.
body.heading: Two fleets and a traffic switch

subtopics.title: Blue/green and managed deployment guardrails

body.body: A canary answers whether the new version is safe; champion/challenger answers whether it is better. The champion is the production model, and one or more challengers receive a fixed share of traffic for long enough to measure business outcomes such as conversion, fraud caught or handling time. This is an experiment, so it needs stable assignment of users or entities to a variant, logging of which model version produced each prediction, and a sample size decided up front. Labels often arrive late, so the comparison window can be days or weeks. In registry terms the two roles map to aliases; when the challenger wins, the champion alias moves and the usual rollout mechanics apply.
body.heading: Comparing outcomes, not just health

subtopics.title: Champion/challenger and online experiments

body.body: Rollback must be faster and simpler than the forward release. Keep the previous version's artifact, image and capacity available until the new one has baked; with GitOps the rollback is a revert of the promotion commit, and with a rollout controller it is an abort that returns traffic to the stable ReplicaSet. Define abort criteria before the release and automate them, since a human watching a dashboard is slow. Models add specific hazards: a new version may need new features or a changed request schema, so keep changes backward compatible for one release; cached or stored predictions from the bad version may need invalidation; and a stateful downstream system may have already acted on bad scores. Record every promotion and rollback against the model version.
body.heading: Make reverting the cheap path

subtopics.title: Designing rollback

concepts.summary: Offline evaluation cannot prove a model behaves well on live traffic, so releases are staged: the new version is exposed to production conditions gradually while automated checks decide whether to continue. Shadow testing gives it real inputs with no user impact, canary and blue/green shift real traffic in controlled steps, and champion/challenger compares business outcomes. Every strategy is paired with a fast, rehearsed rollback.
concepts.title: Staged rollouts: shadow, canary, champion/challenger and rollback

modules.intro: Model release engineering covers the path from a trained artifact to a version serving production traffic: how the model is packaged and versioned, what evidence it must produce before promotion, and how automation moves it through environments. The lessons go from registry and evaluation gates through CI/CD and GitOps to progressive rollout and rollback.
modules.title: Model release engineering

concepts.in_practice: A team typically standardises on one serving stack per workload class: KServe or Ray Serve as the Kubernetes-facing layer, with Triton or a framework runtime underneath for GPU models, and a thin FastAPI service where custom logic is needed. Model owners ship an artifact through the registry; a template renders the serving resource, and a pipeline runs a load test against a staging endpoint before any traffic shift. Capacity is planned per zone, dashboards track p50 and p99 latency, queue time, batch size and accelerator utilisation, and failover is rehearsed by draining a zone during business hours.

sources.title: Ray Serve: Scalable and Programmable Serving

body.body: Online inference answers a request within a latency budget, usually tens to hundreds of milliseconds, and is sized for peak concurrency. Asynchronous inference accepts a request, places it on a queue and returns a handle; workers pull at the rate the accelerators can sustain, which absorbs bursts and suits long-running or large-payload calls. Batch inference scores a whole dataset on a schedule, reads from object storage or a table and writes predictions back, with no endpoint kept alive between runs. The choice is driven by who waits for the answer: a user, another service, or nobody until tomorrow.
body.heading: Three demand shapes

body.body: Each path has a different unit of scaling. Online paths scale on concurrency or request rate and need warm replicas. Queue-driven paths scale on backlog depth and can scale to zero. Batch paths scale on data volume and are judged on cost per million rows and completion time, not on tail latency. A platform normally packages one model image so it can run behind all three paths, keeping preprocessing identical to avoid skew between online and offline predictions.
body.heading: Consequences for the platform

subtopics.title: Request paths: online, asynchronous and batch

body.body: A model server loads artifacts from a model repository, keeps them resident in CPU or GPU memory, and schedules requests onto them. NVIDIA Triton is the reference example: it serves several frameworks side by side (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, Python backends and others), runs multiple instances of a model concurrently, and applies dynamic batching, which holds requests for a short configurable window so that the accelerator executes one larger batch. It exposes HTTP and gRPC endpoints, health and readiness probes, and Prometheus metrics. Ensembles and pipelines let preprocessing, the model and postprocessing run as one server-side graph.
body.heading: What the server does beyond calling predict

body.body: Ray Serve takes a different approach: each step is a Python deployment with its own replica count and resource request, including fractional GPUs, and deployments call each other through handles. This suits pipelines that mix business logic with several models, because composition is ordinary Python and each stage scales independently. It is framework agnostic and supports request batching and response streaming. The trade is that the team owns more of the runtime behaviour than with a fixed-function server.
body.heading: Python-native composition

subtopics.title: Anatomy of a model server

body.body: An inference API needs typed request and response schemas, a model name and version in the path or headers, separate liveness and readiness endpoints (ready only once weights are loaded), and explicit limits on payload size and timeout. FastAPI is a common choice for the thin layer because type-annotated handlers produce validation and OpenAPI documentation automatically. Many servers also implement a standard inference protocol, a shared REST and gRPC shape for tensors and model metadata, so clients do not change when the runtime behind the endpoint changes.
body.heading: The API contract

body.body: On Kubernetes, KServe adds an InferenceService custom resource. The spec names a model format and storage location; the controller selects a serving runtime, pulls the artifact, wires networking, and manages autoscaling, including scale to zero, and canary traffic splitting between revisions. It covers both predictive models and generative models. Platform teams usually wrap this resource in a template so that model owners provide only the artifact location, resources and scaling bounds.
body.heading: KServe as control plane

subtopics.title: Inference API contracts and the serving control plane

body.body: Inference capacity is slow to add: a new replica must schedule onto an accelerator node, pull a large image and load weights, which can take minutes. Designs therefore assume that capacity lost in one zone cannot be replaced instantly. Replicas are spread across availability zones with topology constraints, each zone is sized so that the remaining zones carry peak load, and a second region holds either warm capacity or a smaller fallback. Model artifacts are replicated so that a region can start without reaching into the failed one.
body.heading: Failure modes specific to inference

body.body: When demand exceeds capacity the service should shed load deliberately. Common techniques are bounded queues with early rejection, per-tenant concurrency limits, priority classes that drop batch traffic first, deadline propagation so that expired requests are not executed, and a fallback ladder: a smaller or quantized model, a cached answer, or a rule-based default. Each fallback is tagged in the response so that downstream quality monitoring can separate degraded answers from normal ones.
body.heading: Degrading instead of failing

subtopics.title: Graceful degradation and failover

concepts.summary: Model serving turns a versioned model artifact into an inference API with defined latency, throughput and availability. The architecture splits into a thin API layer, a model server that owns batching and hardware, and a control plane that handles rollout and scaling. The same model is often exposed through several paths (synchronous, asynchronous and batch) because demand shapes differ.
concepts.title: Model serving architecture: inference APIs for batch and real-time demand

concepts.in_practice: Teams define models, endpoint configurations and scaling policies in Terraform, CDK or pipeline code, never in the console. A release pipeline registers the model version, runs a batch transform against a holdout set as an evaluation gate, deploys to a staging endpoint, runs a load test, then updates production with canary traffic shifting and alarm-based rollback. Cost reviews look at instance utilisation per endpoint and move low-traffic models to serverless, asynchronous or shared multi-model hosting.

body.body: Hosting is built from three resources. A Model pairs a container image with a model artifact in S3 and an execution role. An EndpointConfig lists one or more production variants, each naming a model, an instance type, an initial instance count and a traffic weight. An Endpoint is the running, addressable thing created from a configuration; updating it means pointing it at a new configuration. Clients call the runtime API with the endpoint name, and SageMaker routes to healthy instances across availability zones when more than one instance is configured.
body.heading: Model, endpoint configuration, endpoint

body.body: A custom serving container listens on a fixed port and answers two routes: a health check that returns success once the model is loaded, and an invocations route that takes the request body and returns the prediction. The artifact is unpacked into a known directory before the server starts. AWS publishes prebuilt containers for common frameworks and for LLM runtimes, so many teams only write an inference handler. Keeping the same image runnable outside SageMaker makes local testing and later migration much easier.
body.heading: What the container must do

subtopics.title: The endpoint object model and container contract

body.body: Real-time endpoints keep instances running and suit interactive, low-latency traffic with modest payloads. Serverless inference removes instance management and scales to zero, at the price of cold starts and no GPU support, so it fits spiky, low-volume CPU models. Asynchronous inference queues requests, reads large payloads from S3, writes results to S3 and can scale its instances to zero when the queue is empty; it fits long processing times. Batch transform has no persistent endpoint at all: a job starts instances, splits input files from S3 into mini-batches, writes outputs and shuts down.
body.heading: Four options, four demand shapes

body.body: A transform job is tuned with a few parameters: how records are split within a file, how many records go into each request, the maximum payload size and the number of concurrent requests per instance. Input and output can be joined so that predictions sit next to the source record, and filters select which fields reach the model. It is the usual choice for scoring a full dataset, for offline evaluation of a candidate model, and for precomputing predictions that are later served from a database.
body.heading: Batch transform details that matter

subtopics.title: Choosing among real-time, serverless, asynchronous and batch

body.body: Endpoint scaling uses Application Auto Scaling. A production variant is registered as a scalable target with a minimum and maximum instance count, then a policy is attached. Target tracking is the default choice: pick a metric and a target value and the service adds or removes instances to hold it. The predefined metric is invocations per instance; custom metrics such as GPU utilisation or concurrent requests are often better for models whose request cost varies. Step scaling and scheduled scaling cover sharp ramps and known daily patterns.
body.heading: How scaling is configured

body.body: The target comes from a load test, not a guess: find the request rate at which a single instance still meets the latency objective, then set the target below it to leave headroom for the time a new instance takes to come into service. Scale-out cooldown should be short and scale-in cooldown longer, to avoid oscillation. Because new instances must download the image and the artifact, large models need more headroom or a higher minimum count.
body.heading: Finding the target value

subtopics.title: Autoscaling endpoints

body.body: Updating an endpoint uses a blue/green approach by default: a new fleet is provisioned, traffic moves to it, and the old fleet is removed. Traffic can shift all at once, as a canary, or linearly in steps, with a baking period between steps. CloudWatch alarms attached to the update trigger automatic rollback to the old fleet if error rate or latency breaches a threshold. Multiple production variants on one endpoint support weighted A/B tests, and a shadow variant receives a copy of live traffic without returning its responses, which validates a new model or instance type under real load.
body.heading: Deployment guardrails

subtopics.title: Safe updates: variants, traffic shifting and rollback

concepts.summary: Amazon SageMaker offers managed hosting in which AWS runs the instances, load balancing and health management while the team supplies a container and a model artifact. It provides several inference options that map onto online, asynchronous and batch demand. The platform work lies in choosing the right option, wiring autoscaling and making deployments safe and repeatable.
concepts.title: Managed deployment and serving with Amazon SageMaker

concepts.in_practice: A platform team packages each engine as a pinned container image, deploys one model per GPU pool, and fronts everything with a gateway that exposes a single OpenAI-compatible surface with per-tenant keys and token-based rate limits. Before a model is offered, it goes through a benchmark run on the target GPU with production-shaped prompts; the result sets replica limits and the autoscaling threshold. Engine upgrades are treated like model releases, with a canary and a comparison of latency percentiles and output quality on an evaluation set.

sources.title: Efficient Memory Management for LLM Serving with PagedAttention

body.body: A classic model runs one forward pass per request. An LLM runs a prefill pass over the prompt and then one decode step per output token, reusing attention keys and values cached from earlier tokens. That cache grows with sequence length and dominates GPU memory after the weights. Requests have unknown and very different lengths, so static batching wastes capacity. Continuous batching fixes this: the scheduler admits new sequences into the running batch at every decode step and evicts finished ones, so the GPU stays full.
body.heading: Autoregression and the KV cache

body.body: LLM endpoints are measured by time to first token, which reflects queueing plus prefill; inter-token latency, which reflects decode speed under the current batch; and total output tokens per second across all requests, which determines cost. These trade against each other: more concurrency raises throughput and worsens per-request token speed. Objectives are therefore written per metric and per workload, for example interactive chat versus offline summarisation.
body.heading: Metrics that replace plain latency

subtopics.title: Why LLM serving differs from classic model serving

body.body: Earlier systems reserved one contiguous slab of KV cache per request, sized for the maximum possible length. Most of it stayed unused, and free memory fragmented, which capped batch size. PagedAttention, introduced with vLLM, borrows virtual memory paging from operating systems: the cache is divided into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand and mapped through a block table, so blocks need not be contiguous. Waste is limited to the last partial block per sequence. Blocks can also be shared between sequences with copy on write, which helps parallel sampling and beam search. The paper reports throughput gains of roughly two to four times at the same latency against the systems it compared with.
body.heading: The memory problem and the paging answer

body.body: Because memory is pooled, the engine preallocates a fraction of GPU memory at start and admits requests until blocks run out, at which point requests queue or are preempted. Key settings are the memory fraction given to the engine, the maximum context length, and tensor parallelism across GPUs for models that do not fit on one device.
body.heading: Operating consequences

subtopics.title: PagedAttention and vLLM

body.body: SGLang is a serving framework for language and multimodal models with a fast runtime and a set of features aimed at agentic and structured workloads. Its runtime keeps the KV cache of earlier requests and reuses it automatically when a new prompt shares a prefix, which pays off for long system prompts, few-shot templates, multi-turn chat and tool loops. It also provides continuous batching, paged attention, constrained decoding for JSON or grammar-bound output, tensor parallelism and quantized model support.
body.heading: What SGLang adds

body.body: The server is started with a launch command that takes a model path, host and port, and is installed with pip, from source, or as a container image. Server arguments control memory fraction, context length, parallelism, the chat template and API keys. It exposes OpenAI-compatible completion and chat endpoints plus a native generate endpoint, so the same client code works against either engine.
body.heading: Running it

subtopics.title: SGLang: prefix reuse and structured generation

body.body: Both engines speak the OpenAI wire format for chat completions, completions and streaming via server-sent events. Standardising on it lets a gateway route by model name to different engines, apply auth, quotas and token accounting, and swap runtimes without client changes. On Kubernetes each model is a Deployment or serving resource requesting whole GPUs, with weights pulled from object storage or a cache volume to keep start time down, a readiness probe that passes only after the model is loaded, and a generous termination grace period so that in-flight streams finish. Autoscaling keys on queue depth or running requests, not on CPU.
body.heading: The API as the portability layer

subtopics.title: OpenAI-compatible endpoints and Kubernetes deployment

body.body: Benchmark with a prompt and output length distribution drawn from the real workload, since synthetic fixed lengths mislead. Sweep concurrency or arrival rate upward and record time to first token, inter-token latency and total tokens per second at each step; the operating point is the highest load at which the latency objectives still hold. Then change one variable at a time: context length cap, memory fraction, quantized versus full weights, number of GPUs per replica, and prefix caching with a shared system prompt. Record engine version, model revision and GPU type with every result, because releases shift numbers noticeably.
body.heading: A repeatable method

subtopics.title: Benchmarking and tuning an LLM endpoint

concepts.summary: Serving open-weight LLMs is a distinct discipline because generation is autoregressive: each request holds GPU memory for its whole lifetime and produces output token by token. Engines such as vLLM and SGLang exist to pack many concurrent sequences onto a GPU through continuous batching and careful management of the key-value cache. The platform engineer deploys these engines behind an OpenAI-compatible API, benchmarks them and tunes them for a latency and cost target.

concepts.in_practice: Teams add an optimisation stage to the release pipeline after training and evaluation: export, quantize, compile for each target GPU or device class, then rerun the evaluation suite and a latency benchmark on the real hardware. Only variants that hold accuracy within an agreed tolerance and beat the baseline on cost at the latency objective are promoted. Engines are stored as versioned artifacts with build metadata, served through Triton or the bundled server in the data centre, and shipped as signed packages with staged rollout to edge fleets.

body.body: TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's open-source library for optimising LLM inference on its GPUs. It provides a Python API for loading and running models, a command-line server with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and a backend for Triton Inference Server for production serving. Under the hood it applies GPU-specific kernels and graph optimisations together with LLM serving techniques: in-flight batching (its name for continuous batching), a paged KV cache with reuse, multi-GPU execution, and several quantization formats. It also supports speculative decoding and guided decoding.
body.heading: What it is

body.body: An optimised engine is specific to the model, the precision, the shape limits and the GPU architecture it was built for, and is tied to the library version. That makes the build a pipeline stage with its own artifacts: build on the same GPU type that will serve, store the engine in the registry beside the source weights with all build parameters, and rebuild on every model, driver or library upgrade. The reward is typically lower latency and higher throughput than a general-purpose runtime on the same hardware.
body.heading: The cost of compilation

subtopics.title: TensorRT-LLM: compiled engines for NVIDIA GPUs

body.body: Quantization maps floating-point values to low-bit integers with a scale and a zero point, so that a real value is approximately scale times the integer minus the zero point. ONNX Runtime documents three routes. Dynamic quantization computes activation ranges at run time and needs no data, which suits transformer and recurrent models on CPU. Static quantization runs a calibration dataset through the model beforehand to fix the ranges, which is faster at inference and suits convolutional models. Quantization-aware training simulates quantization during training to recover accuracy when the post-training methods lose too much.
body.heading: Core idea and the three methods

body.body: A quantized ONNX model is expressed either with quantized operators or with quantize and dequantize node pairs around normal operators; the second is what accelerator back ends usually consume. Preprocessing the graph with shape inference and fusion before quantizing improves results, and a debugging tool compares tensors between the float and quantized models to find the layers that hurt. For LLMs, common schemes are 8-bit floating point on recent GPUs and 4-bit weight-only methods. Every quantized model must pass the same evaluation gate as the original.
body.heading: Formats and LLM-specific schemes

subtopics.title: Quantization: methods and accuracy control

body.body: Right-sizing for inference starts from a latency objective and a request profile, then compares cost per thousand requests or per million tokens across candidates: CPU instances for small tree and linear models, mid-range GPUs for vision and embedding models, large-memory GPUs for LLMs, and purpose-built inference accelerators where the framework supports them. The deciding numbers come from a benchmark at the latency objective, not from peak throughput. Memory fit is the first filter for LLMs: weights plus KV cache at the intended concurrency must fit, which is where quantization changes the answer. Sharing a GPU among small models through multi-model servers or fractional allocation raises utilisation.
body.heading: Matching hardware to the model

subtopics.title: Right-sizing compute for latency and cost

body.body: Edge targets such as embedded GPU modules, industrial PCs and mobile devices have fixed memory, limited power and thermal headroom, and intermittent connectivity. The usual path is to export the model to an interchange format, quantize it, and run it with a runtime that has an execution provider for the device accelerator; ONNX Runtime and TensorRT are common, and compiled engines must be built for the exact device family. Small language models and vision models are the typical workloads.
body.heading: Constraints and the toolchain

body.body: The platform problem shifts from scaling to fleet management: signed model packages, staged over-the-air rollout by device cohort, on-device version reporting, rollback to the previous model on failed health checks, and buffered telemetry uploaded when connectivity returns. Since ground truth rarely reaches the device, monitoring relies on input statistics and confidence distributions shipped back in summary form. A cloud fallback path handles requests the device model cannot answer within its limits.
body.heading: Operating a fleet

subtopics.title: Edge deployment

concepts.summary: When latency or hardware budget is tight, the model itself is optimised for the target device instead of only scaling the service around it. TensorRT-LLM compiles LLMs into engines tuned for NVIDIA GPUs, quantization reduces the numeric precision of weights and activations to cut memory and compute, and edge deployment pushes the result onto constrained devices. Each step trades flexibility or accuracy for speed, so each needs measurement.
concepts.title: Low-latency inference: TensorRT-LLM, quantization and edge deployment

modules.intro: This module covers how trained models become reliable inference services: the architecture of online and batch serving, the managed route through SageMaker, and the specialised runtimes used for large language models. It moves from general serving patterns to LLM engines and then to compilation, quantization and edge targets, where latency and cost are won.

concepts.in_practice: A team usually starts by enabling a small set of approved models in one or two regions and exposing them through an internal gateway or a thin client library. Access is granted per workload role with IAM, invocation logging is switched on with a retention and redaction policy, and every call carries team and application labels. Prompts live in the repository next to the code that uses them, with a version identifier in the logs. Dashboards show tokens, cost, time to first token and throttle rate per team; quota increases and provisioned capacity are planned from those numbers. Model upgrades are treated as releases: run the eval suite, shadow or canary the new model, then switch the logical model name.

body.body: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers foundation models from multiple providers through one AWS API surface. There is no cluster to operate: a caller names a model identifier and sends a request. For a platform team the value is that the usual AWS controls apply. IAM policies decide which roles may invoke which models, requests can stay on private networking through VPC endpoints, invocations can be logged, and usage lands on the AWS bill where it can be tagged and attributed.
body.heading: A managed model catalog behind AWS controls

body.body: Bedrock separates management operations from inference. The control plane lists models and manages resources such as guardrails, knowledge bases and provisioned capacity. The runtime endpoint is the one applications call for inference. Model availability and quotas differ per region, so a platform must record which model is served from which region, request quota increases ahead of launches, and decide whether cross-region inference is acceptable for the data involved.
body.heading: Control plane and runtime

subtopics.title: How Bedrock exposes foundation models

body.body: The Converse API gives a consistent interface for message-based models. A request carries a model identifier, an optional system prompt, a list of messages with alternating user and assistant roles, and an inference configuration with fields such as maximum tokens, temperature and top-p. Each message holds content blocks, which can be text, images, documents or tool results. Because the shape is the same for every supporting model, swapping models becomes a configuration change, with provider-specific options passed in a separate field.
body.heading: One request shape across models

body.body: Tools are declared with a name, a description and a JSON schema. When the model wants a tool, the response stops with a tool-use stop reason and a content block holding the arguments; the caller runs the tool and sends back a tool result message. The response also reports token usage and latency, which are the raw inputs for cost and performance dashboards. A streaming variant returns incremental events so user interfaces can render text as it is generated.
body.heading: Tool use, stop reasons and streaming

subtopics.title: The Converse API: messages, tools and streaming

body.body: A production prompt has stable parts and variable parts. The system prompt states role, constraints and output format; examples show the expected behavior; retrieved context and the user input are inserted into clearly delimited sections so the model can tell instructions from data. Asking for structured output against a schema, and validating it in code, makes downstream handling deterministic. Lower temperature suits extraction and classification; higher values suit drafting.
body.heading: Structure of a production prompt

body.body: Prompts change behavior as much as code does, so they are stored in version control or a prompt registry, reviewed, and released with an identifier that is logged on every call. A prompt change runs through the same evaluation suite as a model change, because a new model version can break a prompt that was tuned for the old one. Keeping the stable prefix of a prompt identical across calls also makes prompt caching effective where the provider supports it.
body.heading: Versioning and release

subtopics.title: Prompt engineering as an engineering practice

body.body: Cost is driven by input and output tokens, priced per model. Latency has two parts: time to first token, and generation time, which grows with output length. The practical levers are choosing a smaller model for simple tasks, capping output tokens, trimming context, caching repeated prefixes, and moving non-interactive work to batch inference. On-demand capacity is subject to request and token quotas per account and region; steady high-volume workloads can buy provisioned throughput instead.
body.heading: What drives the bill and the latency

body.body: Quota exhaustion shows up as throttling errors, so clients need exponential backoff with jitter, timeouts sized for long generations, and a fallback path to another model or region. Per-team budgets and rate limits stop one tenant from consuming the shared quota. Token counts returned by each call should be emitted as metrics with team, application and model labels, so spend can be attributed and anomalies alerted on before the invoice arrives.
body.heading: Throttling and resilience

subtopics.title: Managing cost, latency and quota at scale

body.body: Most platform teams put a gateway between applications and model providers. Applications call one internal endpoint with a team credential; the gateway maps a logical model name to a provider and model version, applies rate limits and budgets, attaches guardrails, records traces and token usage, and handles retries and failover. This keeps provider keys out of application code and makes it possible to migrate a model, add a provider, or enforce a data policy in one place. The cost is an extra hop and a component that must be highly available, so it is deployed like any other critical proxy: stateless, horizontally scaled, with its own service level objectives.
body.heading: One internal entry point for all model traffic

subtopics.title: The LLM gateway as a platform component

concepts.summary: Hosted LLMs turn model serving into an API integration problem: the platform team does not run GPUs, but it owns access, quotas, cost, latency and the contract that application code uses. Amazon Bedrock exposes foundation models from several providers behind AWS identity and networking, and its Converse API gives one message format across them. Prompts become versioned, tested artifacts, not strings buried in code.
concepts.title: Integrating hosted LLMs: AWS Bedrock, the Claude API and prompt engineering
