concepts.in_practice: Teams run ingestion as a queue-driven or scheduled pipeline with job state in a database, and treat the index as a derived, rebuildable artifact. Each chunk records source, hash and embedding model version, and reindexing into a fresh index with an alias switch is the standard upgrade path. Retrieval is exposed as an internal API or as a tool for agents, with tenant filters applied server side. A golden question set runs in CI and nightly against production indexes; dashboards track retrieval latency per stage, empty-result rate, index lag and embedding spend. Many teams start on Postgres with pgvector or a managed knowledge base and move to a dedicated engine only when measurements require it.

sources.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

body.body: The original RAG work combined a generator, whose knowledge is fixed in its weights, with a dense vector index queried by a neural retriever, and showed that generation conditioned on retrieved passages is more factual and specific. Production systems keep that split but decouple the parts: any embedding model, any vector store, any generator. The design consequence for a platform is that knowledge is updated by reindexing data, not by retraining, and that every answer can carry the identifiers of the passages it was built from.
body.heading: Parametric and non-parametric memory

subtopics.title: The RAG architecture: indexing and query paths

body.body: Once parsing and chunking work, the platform questions are about change. Each chunk should store the source document identifier, a content hash, the chunking version and the embedding model version, so that incremental sync only re-embeds what changed and a model upgrade can be run as a controlled backfill into a new index. Embedding calls are batched and rate limited like any other provider traffic. Deletions must propagate: when a source document is removed or a user loses access, its chunks must disappear from the index within a defined time.
body.heading: Platform concerns beyond parsing

subtopics.title: Ingestion, chunking and embedding pipelines

body.body: pgvector adds a vector column type and distance operators to Postgres: L2 distance, inner product and cosine distance. Without an index a query scans every row, which is exact but slow at scale. Approximate indexes trade recall for speed. HNSW builds a layered graph; it has better query performance and needs no training data, at the cost of slower builds and more memory. IVFFlat partitions vectors into lists and probes a few of them; it builds faster and is smaller, but should be created after the table has data.
body.heading: Exact and approximate search

body.body: Recall is tuned at query time: the HNSW search list size and the IVFFlat probe count both raise recall and latency together. Build-time parameters set graph connectivity or the number of lists. Filters matter: an approximate index applied before a selective metadata filter can return too few rows, so teams use partial indexes, partitioning by tenant, or iterative scan options. Keeping vectors in Postgres gives transactions, joins and row-level security next to the embeddings; dedicated vector databases are chosen when scale or feature needs exceed that.
body.heading: Tuning and filtering

subtopics.title: Vector search and index tuning with pgvector

body.body: After lexical and vector candidates are fused, a common second stage is a cross-encoder reranker that scores each query and passage pair jointly and keeps the top few. It is slower per item, so it runs on tens of candidates, not thousands, and its latency must be budgeted. Query rewriting, which turns a conversational question into a standalone search query, sits before retrieval. Each stage should be measurable on its own: recall at k for retrieval, ranking metrics for the reranker, and groundedness for the final answer.
body.heading: What follows first-stage retrieval

subtopics.title: Hybrid retrieval, fusion and reranking

body.body: A managed knowledge base takes over the indexing pipeline. You point it at a data source, choose an embedding model and a chunking strategy, and it parses, chunks, embeds and writes to a supported vector store, with sync jobs to pick up changes. At query time one API returns the retrieved passages, and another retrieves and generates an answer with citations to the sources. This is a fast path for standard document corpora; custom pipelines remain common where parsing, ranking or access rules are unusual.
body.heading: Bedrock Knowledge Bases

body.body: A shared RAG service needs tenancy and permissions enforced at retrieval time, by metadata filters or separate indexes, because the model cannot be trusted to withhold text it was given. Freshness is a service level objective: time from a source change to a searchable chunk. Quality is tracked with a labeled question set, measuring whether the right passages are retrieved and whether answers are supported by them. Retrieved text is untrusted input and can carry injected instructions, so it is delimited and never granted authority.
body.heading: Access control, freshness and evaluation

subtopics.title: Managed RAG and operating it as a service

concepts.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a model's parametric knowledge with an external, searchable store, so answers can be grounded in current and private data and can cite it. The infrastructure is two pipelines: an offline one that parses, chunks, embeds and indexes documents, and an online one that retrieves, ranks and assembles context for the model. Most quality and reliability problems are data-pipeline and search problems, not model problems.
concepts.title: Retrieval-augmented generation infrastructure and vector search

concepts.in_practice: A platform team usually standardizes three things. First, a tool layer: internal services wrapped as MCP servers, listed in a registry with owners and scopes, reachable over authenticated HTTP. Second, a runtime: an agent loop built on a framework or a workflow engine, with step, cost and time limits, checkpoints, and pause points for human approval of writes. Third, visibility: every model call and tool call is traced with inputs, outputs and cost, and agent behavior is tested with scenario evals before release. New use cases start as a fixed workflow and gain autonomy only where evals show the fixed path is the limit.

body.body: A useful distinction: workflows orchestrate model calls through predefined code paths, while agents let the model direct its own process and tool use. Workflows are more predictable and cheaper; agents handle open-ended tasks where the steps cannot be listed in advance. The standard guidance is to start with a single well-prompted call with retrieval and tools, and add structure only when measurement shows it helps, because each added layer costs latency, money and debuggability.
body.heading: Choosing the simplest structure that works

body.body: Recurring workflow patterns are prompt chaining, where each call consumes the previous output; routing, where a classifier sends input to a specialized path; parallelization, where subtasks or votes run concurrently; orchestrator-workers, where one model splits a task and delegates; and evaluator-optimizer, where one call critiques another in a loop. Frameworks package these, but they also hide prompts and control flow, so teams should be able to see and log exactly what is sent to the model.
body.heading: The pattern vocabulary

subtopics.title: Workflows, agents and the common patterns

body.body: MCP is an open protocol that connects AI applications to external systems. A host is the application the user works in; it creates one client per server connection; a server exposes capabilities. Servers offer three primitives: tools, which are functions the model can call; resources, which are data the application can read into context; and prompts, which are reusable templates. Clients can offer features back to servers, such as sampling, where the server asks the host to run a model call, and elicitation, where it asks the user for input.
body.heading: Roles and primitives

body.body: Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 over a stateful connection. A session starts with an initialize exchange in which both sides declare protocol version and capabilities, so features are negotiated and not assumed. Two standard transports exist: stdio, where the host launches the server as a local subprocess, and Streamable HTTP, for remote servers that many clients share. Remote servers are ordinary network services, so they need authentication, TLS, rate limits, versioning and monitoring like any other internal API.
body.heading: Wire protocol and transports

subtopics.title: Model Context Protocol: hosts, clients and servers

body.body: Tool definitions are prompts: the model chooses and fills them from the name, description and schema alone. Good tools have unambiguous names, parameters that are hard to misuse, descriptions with examples and edge cases, and results that are compact and informative, with errors that say how to recover. Fewer, higher-level tools usually work better than a one-to-one mirror of a REST API, and large results should be paginated or summarized to protect the context window.
body.heading: The agent-computer interface

body.body: Wrapping internal services as MCP servers makes the same tools available to every compliant host, including coding assistants and custom agents. A platform team typically keeps a registry of approved servers with owners, scopes and versions, generates schemas from source where possible, and tests tools against real model behavior, since a schema that compiles can still confuse a model. Reference server implementations are a good starting point for structure and conventions.
body.heading: Publishing tools over MCP

subtopics.title: Designing tools and running a tool catalog

body.body: The MCP specification puts consent with the host: users should understand and approve tool invocations, and tool descriptions from a server are treated as untrusted unless the server is trusted. For remote servers on HTTP transports, the specification defines an authorization model based on OAuth, so a server receives a token scoped to the user and not a shared super-credential. Platform teams add an allowlist of servers, per-tool scopes, audit logs of every call with arguments, and sandboxing for servers that execute code.
body.heading: Protocol-level controls beyond read-only splits

subtopics.title: Permissions, approval gates and MCP authorization

body.body: Beyond durable replay, an agent loop needs explicit bounds: a maximum number of steps, a token and cost budget, a wall-clock limit, and detection of repeated identical tool calls. Context grows with every observation, so runtimes compact history or hand subtasks to sub-agents with fresh context. Agent frameworks supply the loop, state checkpoints and human-in-the-loop pauses; workflow engines supply durable timers and retries around them. The choice between them is mostly about how much control flow the team wants to own.
body.heading: Stopping conditions and frameworks

subtopics.title: Durable, bounded agent runs

concepts.summary: An agent is a model that decides its own next step in a loop of reasoning, tool calls and observations, as opposed to a workflow whose steps are fixed in code. A platform for agents provides the tool layer, the runtime that keeps long runs durable and bounded, and the permission model around actions. The Model Context Protocol standardizes how applications connect models to tools and data, so integrations are written once and reused across hosts.
concepts.title: Agent architectures, agent frameworks and the Model Context Protocol

concepts.in_practice: Teams wire LLMOps into the tooling they already have. A prompt or model change opens a pull request; CI runs the eval suite and posts a score diff; a release tags the prompt and model versions that every trace then carries. In production, traces go through OpenTelemetry to the observability stack or an LLM tracing tool, with redaction at the collector. Guardrails sit at the gateway so every application inherits them, and their intervention rates are on a dashboard next to cost and latency. A weekly review turns flagged traces into new eval cases. For coding assistants, the platform team owns the shared rules, the MCP server allowlist and usage reporting.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

body.body: An eval harness becomes platform infrastructure when it gates releases. The suite runs in CI on any change to a prompt, model identifier, retrieval setting or tool schema, compares scores against the current baseline, and blocks the merge on regression beyond a threshold. Online, a sample of production traffic is scored by the same graders, and user feedback and failed traces are triaged into new cases. Datasets, graders and judge prompts are versioned, since changing any of them changes what a score means.
body.heading: From a harness to a pipeline stage

subtopics.title: Evals as release gates and online checks

body.body: An LLM trace is a tree of spans: the request, each retrieval, each model call and each tool call. Model spans record the model identifier, prompt version, parameters, input and output token counts, time to first token, total latency, stop reason and cost. With that, a bad answer can be replayed step by step, and aggregate views show cost and latency per feature. OpenTelemetry defines semantic conventions for generative AI spans, so traces can flow into an existing observability stack or into an LLM-specific tool.
body.heading: What a trace must contain

body.body: Prompts and completions are the most useful debugging data and the most sensitive. Teams decide per environment whether content is captured in full, redacted or dropped, set retention limits, and restrict who can read traces. Sampling keeps storage in check: keep all errors and flagged outputs, and a fraction of normal traffic. Trace identifiers should be returned to the caller so a user report can be tied to the exact run.
body.heading: Content capture and privacy

subtopics.title: Tracing LLM and agent runs

body.body: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications names the recurring risks. Prompt injection leads the list: text in a user message, a retrieved document or a tool result that the model treats as instructions. Others include sensitive information disclosure, improper handling of model output by downstream code, excessive agency where a model holds more permissions than its task needs, supply chain and data poisoning risks, and unbounded resource consumption. Most mitigations are ordinary security engineering: least privilege, input and output validation, isolation, and limits.
body.heading: The threat model

body.body: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails evaluates both user inputs and model responses against configurable policies: content filters for harmful categories and prompt attacks, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters that block or mask personal data, and contextual grounding checks that flag answers unsupported by the provided source. A guardrail can be attached to model invocations or applied on its own to arbitrary text, so it also works in front of other models. Guardrails add latency and cost per check and produce false positives, so they are versioned, evaluated on a labeled set, and monitored for intervention rate.
body.heading: Managed guardrails

subtopics.title: Guardrails and the OWASP LLM risk list

body.body: Coding assistants run an agent loop inside the editor or terminal: the model searches the codebase, reads files, edits them, runs commands and tests, and iterates on the results. Quality depends on context. Rules files hold persistent instructions that are added to the model context; in Cursor, project rules live in the repository and are version controlled, can be scoped to paths, and sit alongside user-level rules. Claude Code reads a project instruction file in a similar way. Both connect to external tools through MCP servers.
body.heading: How coding agents work

body.body: The platform role is to make assistants productive and safe across teams. That means shared rules that encode conventions, build commands and review expectations; an approved set of MCP servers for internal docs, tickets and read-only infrastructure queries; and permission settings that decide which commands run without confirmation. It also means policy on which code and data may leave the network, usage and cost reporting, and keeping human review and CI gates as the control on what merges.
body.heading: What the platform team standardizes

subtopics.title: AI-assisted development with Cursor and Claude Code

concepts.summary: LLMOps applies the release and operations discipline of MLOps to systems whose behavior is set by prompts, models, retrieval and tools together. The core loop is evaluate before release, trace everything in production, enforce guardrails on inputs and outputs, and feed production failures back into the eval set. The same practices apply to AI coding assistants, which a platform team configures and governs as shared engineering tooling.
concepts.title: LLMOps: evals, tracing, guardrails and AI-assisted development with Claude Code and Cursor

modules.intro: This module covers the platform layer that sits between application teams and large language models: hosted model APIs, retrieval infrastructure, agent runtimes with tool protocols, and the operational discipline that keeps them measurable and safe. It moves from calling a model, to grounding it in data, to letting it act, to proving that all of it works in production.
modules.title: LLM and agent platform

REQS = Counter("inference_requests_total", "Requests",
               ["model", "version", "outcome"])
LAT = Histogram("inference_duration_seconds", "Latency",
                ["model", "version"],
                buckets=[.01, .025, .05, .1, .25, .5, 1, 2.5])

def predict(model, version, x, run):
    with LAT.labels(model, version).time():
        try:

concepts.in_practice: A platform team ships observability as a default, not as a per-team project: a base image or library that configures the OpenTelemetry SDK, a Collector deployed as a DaemonSet plus gateway, and Prometheus scraping every pod that carries the right annotation or ServiceMonitor. Model servers expose a metrics endpoint out of the box, and a GPU exporter runs on every GPU node. Dashboards are generated from templates keyed on model name and version, and recording rules precompute the expensive latency and error ratios that alerts and SLO reports reuse. Cardinality is reviewed like any other cost, because one bad label can take down the metrics store.

body.body: OpenTelemetry defines signals: traces, metrics, logs and baggage. The value comes from correlating them. A resource describes the entity producing telemetry (service name, version, Kubernetes pod, cloud region) and is attached to every signal, so a latency spike in a metric can be narrowed to a pod, then to the traces from that pod, then to the log records that carry the same trace and span ids. For ML services, add the model name and model version as resource or span attributes so every signal can be sliced by the artifact that was actually serving.
body.heading: Beyond three separate tools

subtopics.title: Signals and how they correlate

body.body: A trace is a tree of spans sharing a trace id. Context propagation carries that id across process boundaries, normally in request headers using the W3C Trace Context format, and through message metadata for queues. OpenTelemetry SDKs do this through propagators, and auto-instrumentation libraries cover common HTTP, gRPC and database clients. In an inference path, useful spans are: gateway, feature lookup, preprocessing, queue wait, model execution and postprocessing. Queue wait as its own span is what separates a slow model from an overloaded one.
body.heading: Standard propagation

body.body: Applications export over OTLP to an OpenTelemetry Collector instead of directly to a vendor. The Collector runs receivers, processors and exporters: batching, attribute enrichment from Kubernetes metadata, redaction, and sampling. Tail-based sampling keeps all error and slow traces while dropping most healthy ones, which matters at inference volumes. Running an agent Collector per node plus a gateway Collector deployment is the usual topology, and it lets the backend change without touching application code.
body.heading: The Collector as the pipeline

subtopics.title: Traces, context propagation and the Collector

body.body: Prometheus stores time series identified by a metric name and a set of key-value labels. It collects them by pulling over HTTP from targets it finds through service discovery or static configuration, stores them locally without depending on distributed storage, and exposes them through PromQL. Short-lived jobs that cannot be scraped push through an intermediary gateway. Alerting is evaluated in Prometheus and routed by Alertmanager. Each server is autonomous, which is why it remains usable during the outages you need it for.
body.heading: How Prometheus works

body.body: The instrumentation guidance splits services by type. Online serving systems expose request count, error count and latency. Offline pipelines expose items in and out and time spent per stage. Batch jobs expose the timestamp of the last success, so the alert is on staleness. Use counters for things that only increase and compute rates at query time, gauges for values that go up and down, and histograms for latency so quantiles can be aggregated across replicas. Keep label cardinality bounded: never put user ids, request ids or raw prompts in labels.
body.heading: What to instrument

subtopics.title: Prometheus data model and instrumentation practice

body.body: A model server needs the standard request, error and duration metrics plus dimensions a web service lacks. Track queue depth and queue wait time, batch size distribution, and in-flight requests per replica. For GPUs, export utilization, memory used and temperature per device, mapped to pod and namespace. For LLM serving, track time to first token, tokens generated per second, and input and output token counts, because request latency alone depends on output length. Label by model name and version, not by request content, and record cost drivers such as GPU seconds per tenant so cost can be attributed.
body.heading: What generic service dashboards miss

subtopics.title: Metrics specific to model serving

concepts.summary: Observability is the ability to explain a system's internal state from the telemetry it emits, without shipping new code to ask a new question. For an ML platform this means metrics, logs and traces that are correlated with each other and extended with model-specific dimensions such as model version, queue depth and GPU use. OpenTelemetry standardizes how telemetry is produced and transported, and Prometheus is the common store and query engine for metrics.
concepts.title: Observability: logs, metrics and traces with OpenTelemetry and Prometheus

concepts.in_practice: Teams make monitoring part of the deployment contract: a model cannot be promoted without a registered baseline and a monitoring schedule. Capture is switched on at the endpoint by the platform, a scheduled job (hourly or daily, depending on traffic) computes quality and drift reports, and the summary numbers are exported as metrics next to latency and error rate. Reports with per-feature detail are stored for the investigation that follows an alert. The first weeks after launch are spent tuning thresholds, since default sensitivity produces alerts for seasonal patterns that are not problems. Drift alerts feed the retraining pipeline as a signal, with an evaluation gate before any automatic promotion.

body.body: Data quality monitoring compares live inference inputs with a baseline computed from the training or validation set. In SageMaker Model Monitor a baseline job produces per-feature statistics and a set of suggested constraints: data types, completeness, value ranges and distribution descriptions. A scheduled monitoring job then analyzes captured production data against those constraints and writes a violations report plus metrics that can raise alarms. Typical violations are a missing column, a type change from numeric to string, a jump in null rate, or a category never seen in training. The same pattern works in open source with a reference dataset and a current window.
body.heading: Baseline, constraints, violations

subtopics.title: Data quality monitoring against a baseline

body.body: Data drift, also called covariate shift, is a change in the input distribution. Prediction drift is a change in the output distribution. Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the correct answer, and only labeled data reveals it directly. Managed monitors separate these into data quality, model quality, bias drift and feature attribution drift. Because labels are often late, input and prediction drift act as early proxies for model quality.
body.heading: What can move

body.body: Drift is detected by comparing a reference window with a current window per feature. Common measures are the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for numeric features, chi-squared for categorical ones, and distance scores such as population stability index, Jensen-Shannon divergence or Wasserstein distance. Statistical tests become oversensitive at large sample sizes, so teams usually threshold on a distance score and weight features by importance. For text and embeddings, drift is measured on embedding distributions or with a classifier that tries to tell reference from current data.
body.heading: How it is tested

subtopics.title: Kinds of drift and how they are measured

body.body: Nothing can be monitored unless requests and responses are recorded. Serving endpoints capture a configurable sample of payloads to object storage, each record tagged with an inference id, timestamp, model name and model version. Model quality monitoring needs a later join: the label arrives hours or weeks afterwards from a business system and is matched on the inference id, after which accuracy, precision, recall or error metrics are computed per window. Design points are the sampling rate, redaction of sensitive fields before storage, retention, and partitioning by date and model version so monitoring jobs read only the window they need.
body.heading: The data plumbing

subtopics.title: Capturing inference data and joining ground truth

body.body: Monitoring jobs publish their results as metrics, for example a drift score per feature and a share of drifted features per model. In Prometheus an alerting rule has an expression, an optional for duration that the condition must hold before the alert fires, labels such as severity, and annotations that carry a summary and a runbook reference. The for clause matters because drift scores are noisy between windows. Route by severity: data quality breakage such as a missing feature pages someone, gradual drift opens a ticket, and sustained drift on important features triggers evaluation of a retrained candidate.
body.heading: Turning scores into alerts

subtopics.title: Alerting rules and response

concepts.summary: A model can be up, fast and error-free while its predictions get worse, because the data it sees has moved away from the data it was trained on. Model monitoring adds a second layer on top of service observability: checks on input data quality, on the distribution of inputs and predictions, and on accuracy once ground truth arrives. The outputs are alerts and retraining triggers, not just dashboards.
concepts.title: Model monitoring: data quality, drift and alerting

concepts.in_practice: A platform team writes SLOs per service tier in a short document agreed with the teams that depend on it, encodes the indicators as recording rules, and generates burn-rate alerts from them so nobody hand-writes thresholds. Pages go to a rotation through an incident tool, with a secondary and an escalation path, and each alert links to a runbook kept in the same repository as the service. A weekly review looks at pages received, budget remaining and open postmortem actions. When a budget is exhausted, the agreed policy applies: feature rollouts pause and reliability work takes priority until the service is back inside its objective.

body.body: A service level indicator is a measured quantity, best expressed as a ratio of good events to valid events: requests answered without error, or requests faster than a threshold. A service level objective is a target for that indicator over a window, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days. A service level agreement is a contract with consequences and is normally looser than the internal objective. The error budget is one minus the objective: the amount of failure allowed in the window. When the budget is spent, risky changes slow down, which gives product and platform teams a shared rule.
body.heading: Definitions

body.body: Pick a few indicators that reflect what users experience. For online inference: availability and latency at a high percentile measured at the gateway, not inside the model server. For LLM endpoints: time to first token and successful completion ratio. For batch scoring and feature pipelines: freshness, meaning the share of time the newest output is younger than a threshold, and correctness of the output. Use percentiles, not averages, because averages hide the slow tail. Do not set the target at 100 percent, and do not set it higher than your dependencies can support.
body.heading: Choosing SLIs for ML systems

subtopics.title: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets

body.body: Burn rate is how fast the error budget is consumed relative to a rate that would exhaust it exactly at the end of the window. A burn rate of 1 uses the whole 30-day budget in 30 days. The recommended pattern pages when 2 percent of the budget is consumed in one hour (burn rate 14.4) or 5 percent in six hours (burn rate 6), and opens a ticket when 10 percent is consumed in three days (burn rate 1). Each condition also checks a short window, one twelfth of the long one, so the alert resets quickly after recovery. This gives good precision and recall compared with simple threshold alerts.
body.heading: Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate

subtopics.title: Alerting on SLOs with burn rates

body.body: On-call guidance from site reliability practice caps operational work at half of an engineer's time, keeps the number of incidents per shift low enough that each can be handled and followed up properly, and defines response times by service criticality. Every page must be actionable and linked to a runbook. A runbook for model serving states the symptom, the dashboard to open, the checks in order, and the safe mitigations: roll back to the previous model version, shift traffic away from a canary, scale replicas, fall back to a smaller model or a cached answer. Mitigate first, diagnose after.
body.heading: Sustainable rotations and usable runbooks

subtopics.title: On-call design and runbooks

body.body: A postmortem is a written record of an incident: impact, timeline, root causes, what went well, what went badly, and action items with owners. Triggers are agreed beforehand, for example user-visible downtime beyond a threshold, data loss, a manual rollback, or a monitoring failure. Blameless means the document examines why the system allowed the mistake, not who made it, so people report honestly. Postmortems are reviewed by peers, stored where others can search them, and their action items are tracked to completion. For ML incidents, record the model version, data window and whether monitoring detected the problem before users did.
body.heading: The written review

subtopics.title: Blameless postmortems

concepts.summary: Reliability practice turns the vague goal of a stable service into numbers and routines: service level objectives that define good enough, alerts tied to those objectives, an on-call rotation with runbooks, and postmortems that turn incidents into fixes. For ML platforms the same method applies, with objectives extended to cover freshness and model quality as well as availability and latency.
concepts.title: Reliability practice: SLOs, on-call runbooks and postmortems

concepts.in_practice: Security is built into the paved path so that the secure option is the default one. A new team gets a namespace, a group binding, a service account mapped to a scoped cloud role and a bucket prefix from one request. Pipelines build images on hosted runners, sign them and attach provenance, and an admission policy verifies signatures before anything runs. Secrets come from a secret manager, not from environment files. Model promotion requires an approval recorded in the registry, with lineage and evaluation attached. Access is reviewed on a schedule using last-used data, and audit logs from the cluster and the cloud account flow to a central store the platform team cannot edit.

body.body: RBAC rules are additive only, with no deny rules, so tenant isolation rests on what is never granted. For ML tenants, bind namespaced Roles to groups from the identity provider, not to individual users, and give training operators and pipeline controllers their own service accounts. Watch the permissions that escalate: creating pods lets a subject mount any secret in the namespace, and the bind, escalate and impersonate verbs bypass normal limits. Custom resources for training jobs and inference services need explicit rules, since built-in roles do not cover them.
body.heading: The part specific to ML platforms

subtopics.title: Kubernetes RBAC for ML tenants

body.body: IAM best practice is to remove long-lived keys. Humans sign in through federation with an identity provider and multi-factor authentication, and workloads assume roles that issue temporary credentials. On Kubernetes, a service account is mapped to a cloud role, so a training job receives short-lived credentials scoped to its own bucket prefix and nothing else. Start from the permissions actually used, then tighten: generate policies from access activity, validate them with a policy analyzer, add conditions such as required encryption or source network, and use permission boundaries and organization-wide guardrails so a team admin cannot grant beyond a ceiling. Review and remove unused roles and permissions regularly.
body.heading: Temporary credentials everywhere

subtopics.title: Cloud IAM and workload identity

body.body: SLSA is a specification for securing the path from source to artifact. Its build track defines levels: at level 1 the build produces provenance describing how the artifact was made; at level 2 the build runs on a hosted platform that signs the provenance; at level 3 the platform is hardened so builds are isolated and the signing material is out of reach of the build steps. Consumers verify provenance against expectations before deploying. For ML, apply the same idea to model artifacts: record the training code commit, data snapshot, base image digest and pipeline run, sign the result, and have admission control reject unsigned images or models.
body.heading: Provenance and build levels

subtopics.title: Supply chain integrity with SLSA

body.body: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary framework organized around four functions. Govern sets policies, roles and accountability. Map establishes the context of a system and identifies its risks. Measure analyzes and tracks those risks with quantitative and qualitative methods. Manage prioritizes and acts on them. The platform supplies the evidence: lineage from data to deployed model, model cards, evaluation results, approval records, access logs and monitoring history. Building these as automatic by-products of the pipeline is far cheaper than assembling them for an audit.
body.heading: NIST AI RMF

body.body: LLM applications add an attack surface where untrusted text can steer the model. Treat retrieved documents, tool outputs and user input as data, not instructions. Limit what a model can do through narrowly scoped tool permissions and require human approval for side effects. Run code execution tools in sandboxes with no ambient credentials and restricted network egress. Filter outputs for sensitive data, log prompts and tool calls for audit with redaction, and red-team the system regularly with injection and data exfiltration scenarios, tracking the results as regression tests.
body.heading: LLM-specific controls

subtopics.title: AI risk governance and LLM security

concepts.summary: An ML platform concentrates valuable things: training data, model weights, expensive compute and credentials to many systems. Securing it means giving every human and workload an identity with least privilege, proving where code and model artifacts came from, and running a governance process that manages AI-specific risk. This lesson covers Kubernetes RBAC, cloud IAM, supply chain integrity under SLSA, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.
concepts.title: Security, identity and access, and compliance for ML platforms

flowchart LR
  Q[Queue depth or in-flight requests] --> K[KEDA or HPA]
  K -->|set replicas| D[Model server Deployment]
  D -->|unschedulable pods| KP[Karpenter]
  KP -->|launch| ND[On-demand GPU nodes]
  KP -->|launch| NS[Spot GPU nodes]
  ND --> D
  NS --> D
  KP -->|consolidate idle nodes| X[Removed capacity]
  D --> M[Utilization and cost metrics]
  M --> Q

concepts.in_practice: Teams layer the scalers: KEDA or HPA sets replica counts from queue depth or concurrency, and Karpenter adds or removes nodes in response. Each serving workload gets a minimum replica count sized to the latency objective and a scale-down delay longer than model load time. Load tests establish throughput per replica, which becomes the scaling target. GPU node pools are tainted, capped with limits and split by capacity type, and images and weights are cached on nodes to shorten cold starts. A cost dashboard shows spend and GPU utilization per namespace, reviewed monthly with the owning teams, and commitments such as savings plans are bought only for the steady baseline.

sources.title: Cost Optimization Pillar - AWS Well-Architected Framework

body.body: The HPA controller periodically compares a metric with a target and sets the replica count of a Deployment or StatefulSet. The core calculation is desired replicas equals the ceiling of current replicas times current metric value divided by target value. Resource metrics such as CPU are measured against pod requests, so missing requests break scaling. With several metrics, the largest proposed replica count wins. The behavior field sets stabilization windows and rate limits per direction, which is how flapping is prevented.
body.heading: The control loop

body.body: A GPU model server can be saturated while its CPU sits low, so scale on a signal that tracks load: in-flight requests per replica, queue depth, or GPU utilization exposed through a custom or external metrics adapter. Scale up fast and down slowly, because a new replica must pull a large image, load weights and warm up before it is useful. Readiness probes must pass only after the model is loaded, otherwise traffic reaches pods that cannot answer and latency objectives are missed during every scale-up.
body.heading: Why CPU is the wrong signal for inference

subtopics.title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

body.body: KEDA is an event-driven autoscaler that extends Kubernetes instead of replacing the HPA. A ScaledObject names a workload and one or more triggers, called scalers, that read an external source: queue length, stream lag, a Prometheus query, a schedule. KEDA activates the workload from zero when events appear and feeds metrics to an HPA it manages for scaling from one upward. A ScaledJob instead starts a Job per batch of events, which suits long-running work that must not be interrupted. This fits asynchronous inference, batch scoring and rarely used models, where idle GPU pods would otherwise cost money.
body.heading: Scaling from external signals and to zero

subtopics.title: Event-driven scaling with KEDA

body.body: Karpenter watches for pods the scheduler cannot place and launches nodes sized to fit them, reading their resource requests, node selectors, affinities, tolerations and topology spread. A NodePool sets constraints such as allowed instance families, zones, capacity type and limits on total resources, and a NodeClass holds cloud-specific settings such as images and networking. Disruption handling removes or replaces nodes that are empty, underused, drifted from their specification or past an expiry, respecting pod disruption budgets.
body.heading: Just-in-time nodes

body.body: Spot capacity is much cheaper but can be reclaimed at short notice. Put interruptible work on it: training with checkpointing, batch inference, hyperparameter sweeps. Keep latency-critical serving on on-demand or reserved capacity, or run a baseline on-demand with burst on spot. Allow many instance types so the provisioner can find available capacity. Use separate NodePools with taints for GPU nodes so only GPU workloads land there, and protect long training pods from voluntary consolidation.
body.heading: Spot and on-demand mix

subtopics.title: Node provisioning with Karpenter and spot mix

body.body: Right-sizing for ML starts with GPU duty cycle and memory headroom, since an allocated but idle GPU is the largest waste. Raise utilization through dynamic batching, running several model replicas per device, GPU sharing by time slicing or hardware partitioning, and choosing the smallest GPU type that meets the latency objective. Then measure unit cost: cost per thousand inferences, per million tokens or per training run, attributed to teams by namespace and labels. The cost optimization pillar frames this as ongoing practice: financial ownership, expenditure awareness, cost-effective resources, matching supply to demand, and optimizing over time.
body.heading: The GPU-specific part

subtopics.title: Right-sizing, GPU utilization and cost attribution

concepts.summary: ML workloads are expensive and bursty, so capacity has to follow demand at two levels: the number of pods and the number and type of nodes under them. Kubernetes HPA and KEDA scale pods, Karpenter provisions and consolidates nodes, and cost practice decides what is right-sized, what runs on spot capacity and how GPU time is kept busy. The goal is to meet latency objectives at the lowest cost per unit of useful work.
concepts.title: Autoscaling and cost efficiency: right-sizing, spot mix and GPU utilization

Each lesson starts from the operating principle and then moves to the concrete tools and configuration a platform team uses.
modules.title: Operating ML in production

diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  U[ML engineer] --> P[Developer portal]
  P --> T[Software template]
  T --> R[New repository from skeleton]
  T --> C[Catalog entry with owner]
  R --> CI[CI build and tests]
  CI --> G[GitOps deploy]
  G --> K[Platform runtime]
  K --> O[Dashboards and alerts]

concepts.in_practice: A platform team usually starts by picking the one or two workload shapes that most teams ship, such as a batch training pipeline and an online endpoint, and builds a template for each that produces a deployable repository in minutes. The template lives in a portal, most often Backstage, alongside the catalog and documentation, and it calls the same CI, GitOps and infrastructure modules the platform team uses itself. The team then onboards a friendly pilot team, watches where they get stuck, fixes the template and documentation, and only then advertises the path widely. Templates are versioned, changes are reviewed like product changes, and a dashboard tracks adoption and time to first deployment so the roadmap is driven by evidence.

body.body: The CNCF platforms white paper describes a platform as a curated set of capabilities offered to internal users through consistent interfaces, run by a team that treats those users as customers. For an ML platform the capabilities are things like compute for training, pipeline orchestration, artifact and model storage, serving, observability and identity. The product stance means the team does user research, publishes a roadmap, writes documentation as a first-class deliverable and keeps adoption optional where it can, so that usage is a real signal. The platform team aims to reduce cognitive load: a data scientist should need to understand the model and the contract of the platform, not the cluster, the network and the IAM layout underneath it.
body.heading: What changes when users are internal customers

body.body: Start with the smallest set of capabilities that removes a real, repeated pain, often just a template, a CI pipeline and a documented deploy path. Wrap existing provider services instead of rebuilding them, and add abstraction only where several teams hit the same friction. Each capability needs an owner, a support channel and a stated service level, otherwise it is a shared script and not a product.
body.heading: Thinnest viable platform

subtopics.title: Treating the platform as a product

body.body: A golden path is the supported, opinionated route from idea to production for one kind of workload: for example a batch training job, a real-time model endpoint or a feature pipeline. It bundles a repository skeleton, a build and test pipeline, deployment manifests, default dashboards and alerts, and the security settings the organization requires. The path is paved, not walled: teams can leave it, but then they own what the platform would have given them for free.
body.heading: What a golden path is

body.body: Backstage Software Templates implement this with a Template entity. The parameters section declares a form, rendered in the portal, that collects inputs such as service name, owner and model type. The steps section runs scaffolder actions in order: fetch a skeleton and render it with the inputs, publish the result to a new repository, and register the new component in the catalog. Custom actions can add steps such as creating a namespace, an experiment in the tracking server or a pipeline definition.
body.heading: Scaffolding with Backstage templates

subtopics.title: Golden paths and software templates

body.body: Backstage is an open framework for building developer portals. Its center is the software catalog: every service, library, pipeline, dataset or model is described by a small metadata file kept next to the code, stating its kind, owner, lifecycle and relations to other entities. The portal ingests those files and gives a searchable inventory with ownership attached. Around the catalog sit TechDocs, which renders documentation written beside the code, and a plugin system that surfaces CI status, deployments, cost or on-call data on the entity page. For an ML platform the useful extension is modeling ML-specific entities, so a served model links to its training pipeline, its registry entry, its feature sources and the team that answers the page.
body.heading: One place to find and own things

subtopics.title: The developer portal and software catalog

body.body: A typical ML path starts with a template that creates a repository with a standard project layout, a container build, unit tests and a pipeline definition. Training runs through the platform orchestrator, logs parameters and metrics to the tracking server and writes a versioned artifact to the model registry. A promotion step runs evaluation gates, then a GitOps change deploys the model to the serving layer with a staged rollout. Dashboards, alerts, drift monitors and cost labels are created by the path, not by the team.
body.heading: From template to serving endpoint

body.body: The interface is usually a short declarative spec: model name, framework, resource class, scaling bounds and data dependencies. The platform expands it into the full Kubernetes or cloud resources. Keep an escape hatch, such as an overlay or raw manifest patch, so unusual workloads are possible without forking the path. Version the templates and provide an upgrade mechanism, because generated repositories drift from the template the day after they are created.
body.heading: Choosing the abstraction level

subtopics.title: Anatomy of an ML golden path

body.body: Measure the platform the way a product is measured. Useful signals include the share of workloads on the golden path, time from template creation to first production deployment, deployment frequency and failure rate for path users, the number of support tickets per team and how many requests still need a human on the platform team. Developer surveys add the qualitative side. Recurring support questions are the backlog: each one is a candidate for better documentation, a clearer error message, a new template parameter or a new capability. Office hours, an open support channel and embedding with a user team for a sprint are common ways to see friction first hand. Deprecate paths that nobody uses, since every supported path carries maintenance cost.
body.heading: Signals that the platform works

subtopics.title: Measuring adoption and closing the feedback loop

concepts.summary: A self-service platform lets ML and product teams get a working, compliant project, pipeline or endpoint without filing a ticket. The platform team packages its opinions as golden paths: templates, a catalog and a small set of well-documented interfaces that make the supported way the easiest way. The work is treated as product management as much as engineering, with users, feedback and adoption metrics.
concepts.title: Self-service platforms: golden paths, templates and developer tooling

diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  A[Tenant A requests] --> GW[Gateway with per-tenant rate limits]
  B[Tenant B requests] --> GW
  GW -->|over limit| REJ[Fast reject]
  GW --> Q[Bounded queue with criticality]
  Q -->|overload| SHED[Shed low priority]
  Q --> ADM[Admission and quota check]
  ADM --> NSA[Namespace A quota and policies]
  ADM --> NSB[Namespace B quota and policies]
  NSA --> GPU[Shared GPU node pool]
  NSB --> GPU
  GPU --> COST[Usage and cost by tenant label]

concepts.in_practice: Teams usually begin with one namespace per team and environment, stamped out by automation with RBAC bindings, a default deny network policy, a ResourceQuota, a LimitRange and cost labels. GPU nodes sit in dedicated pools behind taints, and a batch queueing layer handles guaranteed shares, borrowing and preemption for training jobs. Shared services such as the inference gateway, the tracking server and the orchestrator enforce per-tenant rate and concurrency limits and return fast rejections when saturated, with clients configured for bounded, jittered retries. Utilization and cost per tenant are reviewed regularly, quotas are adjusted from data, and the design is load tested with one deliberately abusive tenant to confirm others stay within their service objectives.

sources.title: Machine Learning Lens - AWS Well-Architected Framework

body.body: Kubernetes documentation distinguishes multi-team tenancy, where tenants are teams inside one organization, from multi-customer tenancy, where tenants are external and untrusted. The basic unit is the namespace: RBAC roles are bound per namespace, quotas attach to it and most policies are scoped by it. A common convention is one namespace per team and environment, created by automation with the same baseline every time. When tenants need their own cluster-scoped resources, such as custom resource definitions, namespaces are not enough and teams move to virtual control planes or a cluster per tenant.
body.heading: Control plane isolation

body.body: Workloads share nodes, a network and a kernel unless told otherwise. NetworkPolicy with a default deny rule stops cross-namespace traffic. Pod Security Standards block privileged containers. Dedicated node pools with taints and tolerations keep one tenant's pods off another's nodes, which matters for GPU nodes and for sensitive data. Sandboxed runtimes add a stronger boundary for untrusted code such as user notebooks. Storage isolation comes from per-tenant buckets or prefixes with scoped identities.
body.heading: Data plane isolation

subtopics.title: Tenancy models and isolation layers

body.body: A ResourceQuota caps the aggregate consumption of one namespace: total CPU and memory requests and limits, storage requests, object counts such as pods or services, and extended resources such as GPUs through a requests-prefixed resource name. When a quota for CPU or memory is active, every new pod must declare that value or it is rejected, so a LimitRange is normally added to supply defaults. Quotas can be scoped, for example by PriorityClass, so a tenant gets a small allowance of high priority pods and a larger one of preemptible pods. Quota is enforced at admission and does not affect pods already running.
body.heading: ResourceQuota and LimitRange

body.body: Static quotas strand capacity: a team that is idle still holds its GPUs on paper. Batch queueing systems add borrowing, where a tenant can exceed its guaranteed share while others are idle and is preempted when the owner returns. Design decisions include guaranteed versus burst share, preemption order, and whether jobs are admitted all at once so distributed training does not start with half its workers.
body.heading: Beyond static quotas

subtopics.title: Quotas, limits and fair sharing of compute

body.body: The SRE book treats overload as something every service must plan for. Capacity should be measured in real resource cost, not raw request count, since requests differ widely in cost; for model serving this means tokens or GPU seconds. Each tenant gets a per-customer limit, and requests over the limit are rejected early and cheaply instead of queuing. Requests carry a criticality label so that under pressure the service sheds low priority traffic, such as batch scoring, before interactive traffic. Rejecting is better than degrading everyone.
body.heading: Per-tenant limits and load shedding

body.body: Rejections still cost the server something, so clients throttle themselves: adaptive throttling tracks requests sent against requests accepted and starts dropping locally when the ratio grows. Retries need budgets, both per request and per client, or a small overload becomes a retry storm that spreads through layers. In ML platforms the same ideas apply to bounded queues in front of inference servers, admission limits on pipeline submissions and concurrency caps per tenant on the orchestrator.
body.heading: Client behavior and retries

subtopics.title: Backpressure and overload handling on shared services

body.body: The AWS Well-Architected Machine Learning Lens applies the cost optimization pillar across the ML lifecycle: tag resources, right-size training and inference, and choose pricing models to match workload behavior. On a shared platform this starts with mandatory labels for team, project and environment, injected by the golden path and enforced by admission policy, so every pod, volume and endpoint maps to an owner. Showback reports spending per tenant; chargeback bills it. Shared costs such as the control plane, idle GPU headroom and the platform's own services need an explicit allocation rule. Typical levers are interruptible capacity for fault-tolerant training with checkpointing, scale to zero for idle endpoints, smaller or quantized models for cost-sensitive serving, and quota sized from measured utilization.
body.heading: Making cost visible per tenant

subtopics.title: Cost attribution and capacity trade-offs per tenant

concepts.summary: A shared ML platform runs training, batch and serving workloads from many teams on common clusters and accelerators. The design problem is to give each tenant isolation, a fair and predictable share of scarce capacity, and protection from other tenants under overload. This lesson covers the isolation layers, quota and fairness mechanisms, backpressure patterns and cost attribution that make sharing safe.
concepts.title: System design for multi-tenant ML infrastructure: isolation, quotas and backpressure

code.code:
# ADR 0012: Use a batch queue for GPU training jobs

## Status
Accepted (supersedes ADR 0007)

## Context
Static namespace quotas leave GPUs idle while other
teams wait. Distributed jobs start partially scheduled.

## Decision
Admit training jobs through a queueing layer with
guaranteed shares, borrowing and preemption.

## Consequences
- Higher GPU utilization; borrowed jobs can be preempted.
- Jobs must checkpoint to tolerate preemption.
- One more controller to operate and upgrade.

flowchart LR
  P[Problem identified] --> D[Draft design doc]
  D --> S[Small group feedback]
  S --> W[Wider review window]
  W -->|open concerns| D
  W --> A[Approvers sign off]
  A --> R[ADR recorded in repo]
  R --> I[Implementation and rollout]
  I -->|decision changes| N[New ADR supersedes old]

concepts.in_practice: A platform team keeps a docs or decisions directory in its main repository with numbered ADR files and a template, and requires a design doc for any change that adds a capability, alters a tenant-facing interface or is costly to reverse. The author writes a draft, shares it with two or three close reviewers, then opens it to affected user teams for a fixed comment window. Named approvers sign off, the key decisions are extracted into ADRs, and the doc is linked from the tracking issue and the catalog entry. Larger changes add a rollout and rollback section modeled on enhancement proposals. Superseded records stay in place with a pointer to their replacement, so new engineers can read the history instead of asking for it.

sources.title: Google Engineering Practices: How to do a code review

body.body: As described in the account of design docs at Google, a design doc is a relatively informal document written before coding that records the high level implementation strategy and the key decisions, with emphasis on the trade-offs considered. A common shape is: context and scope, goals and non-goals, the actual design, alternatives considered and cross-cutting concerns such as security, privacy and observability. Non-goals are things that could reasonably be goals but are explicitly excluded. The design section usually opens with an overview and a system context diagram, then covers APIs and data storage at sketch level, not full schemas or code.
body.heading: Structure and intent

body.body: The doc pays off when the solution is ambiguous, the cost of a wrong turn is high or several teams must agree. If the design is obvious, a doc that only restates the implementation is overhead. Length should match the problem: larger efforts land around ten to twenty pages, while an incremental change can use a mini doc of one to three pages.
body.heading: When to write one

subtopics.title: Anatomy of a design doc

body.body: An architecture decision record captures a single architecturally significant decision together with its context and consequences. The widely used template has a title, a status such as proposed, accepted, deprecated or superseded, the context that forced the decision, the decision itself and the consequences, including the negative ones. Records are numbered, kept as text files in the repository next to the code they govern and reviewed through pull requests. An accepted record is not rewritten when the decision changes: a new record supersedes it and links back, so the collection becomes a decision log that explains why the system looks the way it does.
body.heading: One decision per record

body.body: Good candidates are choices that are expensive to reverse: the orchestrator, the model registry, the tenancy model, the serving runtime, how features are stored, how secrets and identities are issued. Record the options rejected and the evidence used, such as a benchmark or a cost estimate, since that is what future readers ask about.
body.heading: What deserves an ADR on an ML platform

subtopics.title: Architecture decision records

body.body: The Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal template shows what a heavier process looks like for changes that many users depend on. Besides summary, motivation, goals, non-goals and the proposal itself, it requires risks and mitigations, design details, a test plan, graduation criteria from alpha through beta to stable, an upgrade and downgrade strategy, a version skew strategy, a production readiness questionnaire, drawbacks and alternatives. The production readiness section asks how the feature is enabled and rolled back, how operators know it is working and what it depends on. An ML platform team can borrow a trimmed version for changes that touch every tenant, such as a new pipeline API version or a cluster migration.
body.heading: The KEP template as a model

subtopics.title: Enhancement proposals for platform-wide changes

body.body: Google's code review guidance puts design first among the things to examine, ahead of functionality, complexity, tests and naming, and sets the standard that a change should be approved once it clearly improves overall health, even if it is not perfect. The same standard carries over to design review. Check that the problem and non-goals are stated, that the simplest design that meets the goals was considered, that alternatives were rejected for real reasons, and that failure modes, migration, security and operating cost are addressed. Separate blocking concerns from preferences, explain the reasoning behind each comment and respond quickly, since a stalled review stalls the project.
body.heading: What a reviewer looks for

body.body: Share drafts early with a small group, then widen. Use comments for detail and a short meeting only for unresolved disagreement. Name the approvers up front, record the outcome and update the doc when implementation diverges.
body.heading: Running the process

subtopics.title: Reviewing design docs and decisions

concepts.summary: Platform decisions outlive the people who made them and affect every team on the platform, so they need a written record that can be reviewed before work starts. Design docs explain a proposed system and its trade-offs, architecture decision records capture single decisions and their consequences, and enhancement proposals add rollout and operational rigor. Reviewing these documents well is a skill of its own.
concepts.title: Writing and reviewing design docs and architecture decision records

modules.intro: An ML platform succeeds only if teams choose to use it, so this module treats the platform as a product with users, paved paths and measurable adoption. It then covers the system design needed to share that platform safely across many tenants, and the written decision process that keeps its architecture coherent.
